v: On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, of the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
b: Jesus took the initiative to find Philip and said to him, “Follow me.” This statement reveals the heart of the calling: it is not a set of religious requirements or a job assignment, but an invitation into a relationship of walking together. What the Lord wants has never been our achievements, but our hearts, our willingness to be led by Him and to walk with Him. Following is not a matter of analysis but of trust; not of relying on ourselves but of being willing to let the Lord rule.

As soon as Philip met Jesus, the first thing he did was find Nathanael. A person who has truly met the Lord does not want to keep it to himself, but longs to bring others to the Lord. Philip shared in a way Nathanael could understand: “We have found him of whom Moses in the law and the prophets wrote!” He did not yet fully understand all of Jesus, but he shared what he knew, and that was enough. God does not require us to be perfect, only faithful, bringing people to Him.

Nathanael's first reaction, however, was doubt: “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” He was limited by his own preconceptions, prejudices, and judgments. He thought God would not accomplish great things through an unremarkable place or an ordinary background. Yet God often works in the least remarkable places and often shows His glory through people we think impossible.

Philip did not argue or debate. He simply said, “Come and see.” He did not persuade with eloquence or overwhelm with theory, but invited Nathanael to meet Jesus personally and see who the Lord really is. Only when we see for ourselves and face the Lord personally are prejudices broken, hearts truly softened, and lives turned around. True leading is not persuading, but bringing people to the Lord and letting Jesus Himself change them.
q: Are there “Nazareth”-type prejudices in your life that make it hard for you to believe God can work there? Today, will you say to the Lord, “I am willing to come and see”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for taking the initiative to call us and invite us to follow You. Make us like Philip, bringing people to Jesus, and like Nathanael, laying down prejudice and opening our hearts to meet You. May we not rely on our own judgment but be willing to “come and see,” experiencing Your reality and glory for ourselves. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!”
Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!”
Jesus answered him, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you underneath the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these!”
He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
b: While Nathanael was still doubtful about Jesus, the Lord had already seen him and known him, and He gave His verdict on what was truly in his heart: “in whom is no deceit.” Jesus does not look at appearance, background, or manner of speech, but at the true condition of a person's heart. Although Nathanael had prejudices, he was honest, without pretense or hypocrisy. A genuine heart attracts the Lord's eyes more than a perfect exterior.

Nathanael asked in amazement, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” These words touched Nathanael deeply, because that was a place only he knew. Jesus knew not only where he was, but also his heart, his prayers, and his struggles. The Lord's seeing goes far beyond human sight; He sees how we act among people, and He sees the thoughts and intentions of our hearts in secret. Nothing can be hidden from Him.

At that moment Nathanael's prejudice collapsed completely, and he immediately declared, “You are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!” When a person truly meets Jesus, there is no need for debate or persuasion; the heart naturally yields before His reality. True faith comes not from analysis but from meeting the Lord.

Jesus then said, “You will see greater things than these.” Knowing the Lord never stops at first impressions; the more we follow Him, the more we see His glory, His greater works, and deeper revelation. Finally He declared, “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.” This shows that Jesus is the only way between heaven and earth, the revelation of God's presence, and the only way people can truly meet the Father. He is not only our Savior but also the gate of heaven, the One through whom God's work is made known on earth.
q: What are the hidden “under the fig tree” places in your life? Believing the Lord has already seen, will you come before Him once more with an honest heart?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You saw us before we saw You. Make our hearts as pure as Nathanael's, without hypocrisy or pretense, so that when we meet Jesus we may surrender completely. May the more we follow You, the more we see heaven opened and see Your greater works. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: The third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there.
Jesus also was invited, with his disciples, to the wedding.
When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.”
His mother said to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.”
b: The wedding at Cana was the first sign of Jesus' public ministry. It took place not in a synagogue or a religious gathering, but in a home, at a wedding, in a setting very close to ordinary people. God does not work only in the temple; He is willing to show His glory in people's daily lives, in the most ordinary places. Jesus' attending the wedding shows that He does not stay far from people's joys and needs; He is willing to walk into our homes and our daily lives, making the ordinary a stage for miracles.

“They ran out of wine” was the most embarrassing, shameful, and helpless moment of a wedding. In life we too often meet situations where “the wine has run out”: our energy runs out, our love runs out, our patience runs out, the spark in a marriage runs out, the warmth in a parent-child relationship runs out, our faith runs out, our direction runs out. Yet precisely in such bottlenecks, our lack becomes the opportunity for the Lord to step in. When we can do nothing on our own, God's grace has room to work, and He can turn lack into abundance and crisis into blessing.

Mary said to Jesus, “They have no wine.” This is a heart that brings the problem to Jesus. She did not command Jesus or direct what He should do; she simply entrusted the need to the Lord. Jesus reminded her, “My hour has not yet come.” His works are not driven by human urging but follow the Father's timing. God's timing is always exact; waiting is not delay but the prelude to God revealing His glory.

Mary told the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.” These words reveal the key to the miracle: obedience. Not our own methods, not human analysis, but wholehearted obedience to the Lord's leading. When people are willing to hand sovereignty to Jesus and do as He says, miracles flow naturally from acts of obedience.
q: In which area of your life is the “wine running out”? Are you willing to bring this need to Jesus and be ready to “do whatever He says”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for entering our lives, for being our provision when we lack and our strength when we are weak. Give us hearts willing to entrust and obey, so that we are not impatient while waiting for You and act at once when we hear Your word. May Your works be seen in our homes, our lives, and our hearts. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece.
Jesus said to them, “Fill the water pots with water.” So they filled them up to the brim.
He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it.
When the ruler of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom
and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!”
This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
b: The six stone water jars were originally prepared for the rites of purification, representing human effort, human rules, and human ways. They were a religious symbol of people trying to reach holiness through their own works. Yet although these jars seemed useful, they could not supply the real need; they were empty inside and could hold only water, not bring life, joy, and renewal. God often begins to work exactly where “we have used up all our own methods and are still empty.”

Jesus told the servants, “Fill the water pots with water.” This seemed completely illogical, because what was lacking was not water but wine. But obedience does not wait until we understand; it begins by doing what the Lord says. The servants filled the jars “to the brim,” a complete obedience: holding nothing back, cutting no corners, and doing no calculations for God. They did not know what would happen next, but their hearts were ready to believe and do as told.

Then Jesus said, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” This step required even more faith. What they drew out was “water,” yet they were to carry it as “wine.” This meant they had to take a step of faith, willing to obey before seeing the miracle. They experienced God's work in their obedience, and the miracle came through their act of faith.

After tasting it, the ruler of the feast marveled, “You have kept the good wine until now!” In human eyes the best should come first, but with God, what comes later is always better than what came before. He does not patch up the old; He brings in the very best, turning lack into abundance and shame into glory.

This was the first sign Jesus performed, the beginning of His public ministry. The sign revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him more deeply. As He works in our lives, our faith too is lifted again and again, so that we see more of His reality and great power.
q: What are the “fill the jars” and “draw it out” the Lord asks of you today? Are you willing to obey His leading before you see the result?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for beginning Your work where we are lacking. Give us obedient hearts, willing to fill the jars, willing to draw out and carry it, willing to trust and follow You where we cannot see. Bring the best into our lives, so that people may see Your glory. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: After this, he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and they stayed there a few days.
The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
He found in the temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting.
He made a whip of cords, and threw all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the changers’ money and overthrew their tables.
To those who sold the doves, he said, “Take these things out of here! Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!”
His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up.”
b: After leaving the wedding, Jesus stayed briefly in Capernaum and then went up to Jerusalem for the Passover. This festival was Israel's great day of remembering God's redemption, when people should come to the temple with reverence, gratitude, and longing. But when Jesus entered the temple, what He saw was not worship but buying and selling, noise, and trading for profit. The temple, which was meant to be God's dwelling place and a house of prayer, had become a place of commerce and gain.

Jesus took a startling action: He made a whip of cords, drove out the sheep and cattle, overturned the tables, poured out the coins, and cleared out everything the merchants had. He was not losing His temper; with holy anger He was defending His Father's house. His voice was loud and clear: “Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!” The place where God dwells cannot be mixed with selfishness, scheming, and the trading of favors.

This passage also invites us to reflect: our hearts are now the temple of the Holy Spirit. Are we letting the noise of the world, our selfish desires, calculation, and bargaining occupy them? Sometimes we come before God not to worship but with a bargaining mindset: give me this, help me with that, accomplish my plans. If we are centered not on God but on ourselves, then the temple of our heart is defiled just as the temple was then, and needs Jesus Himself to come and cleanse it.

The Lord's cleansing is not meant to shame us but to restore us, so that we can once again come close to Him with reverence and wholehearted love. He is willing to pour out the clutter in our hearts and remove motives that should not be there, so that we return to our rightful place: letting God be God, letting us be human, and letting Him reign in our hearts.

Seeing all this, His disciples remembered what was written: “Zeal for your house will eat me up.” This is the heart of Jesus: He longs for our hearts to be prepared for God alone, undisturbed by impurities and unaffected by the world's trading mindset. He is willing to kindle a fire within us, so that our hearts are once again drawn to Him, cleansed by Him, and renewed by Him.
q: Today, if Jesus walked into the temple of your heart, which “tables” would He clear? Will you let Him cleanse you so that He may have full rule?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, cleanse our hearts so that we do not come before You with a bargaining mindset, but with reverence, trust, and obedience. Remove from our hearts every motive that does not belong to You, so that we may let You alone be King. May Your temple be restored in our hearts as a place of prayer and worship. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: The Jews therefore answered him, “What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?”
Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
The Jews therefore said, “It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?”
But he spoke of the temple of his body.
When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he said this, and they believed the Scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.
b: After Jesus cleansed the temple, the religious leaders challenged Him: “What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?” What they wanted was outward proof, a visible miracle, evidence that could be measured, but they were unwilling to admit that they had drifted far from God and that the temple had been defiled. They cared about form rather than spiritual reality, about the source of authority rather than God's heart.

Jesus' answer was deeply prophetic: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews immediately thought of the magnificent temple before them, which had taken forty-six years to build, and assumed Jesus was speaking of a physical building. People's thinking is often limited by the surface; they look at the outward and the visible. But the temple Jesus spoke of was His own body, a true revelation that He would lay down His life for the world and rise on the third day.

People thought Jesus was talking about rebuilding a building, but Jesus was talking about the completion of redemption; people were concerned with a temple of piled stones, but Jesus was concerned with the temple where God and people are restored together: Himself. With His body He established a new way of worship, a new way, so that people no longer need to rely on human systems but can come directly to the Father through Him.

Only after Jesus was raised from the dead did His disciples remember what He had said. They suddenly understood: Jesus had long ago foretold His death and resurrection, and had long ago revealed that He is the new temple, the everlasting link between people and God. When the Lord's resurrection became a fact, their faith was no longer a doctrine they had heard but a truth they had seen, and so “they believed the Scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.”

Sometimes we do not understand God's word at the moment, but if we keep following, at some point He will make it suddenly clear. His works often exceed human understanding, but when He fulfills them, we see His wisdom and faithfulness. The Lord's word is always trustworthy. Even when we cannot see, touch, or work it out at the moment, if we trust and obey Him, He will bring His word to pass in His own time.
q: Are you willing to believe God's promises even when you still cannot understand them? Which word of the Lord in your life needs to be remembered and believed again?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for making Jesus the true temple, so that through Him we can come to You. Help us not to be limited by outward things, but to listen with our hearts to Your voice and believe what You have said. When we do not understand, give us faith to wait until You make it clear to us Yourself. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he did.
But Jesus didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone,
and because he didn’t need for anyone to testify concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man.
b: Many people believed in Jesus because they saw the signs, which seems a good thing, yet Jesus “didn’t trust himself to them.” Outward enthusiasm, amazement, and emotional belief are not the same as true faith. Only faith in which the heart is truly enlightened by God and surrenders can last, can follow, and can endure trials. Miracles can draw people near but cannot make them take root; only a real relationship with the Lord lets faith stand firm.

Jesus knew all people, and He knew what was in man. He knows that people are easily moved by outward emotion while the heart is not truly entrusted; that people are easily drawn by miracles but unwilling to let Him be King; that people cry out, “I will follow you,” but draw back when the storms come. What Jesus sees is the motives, desires, weaknesses, and hidden corners deep in a person's heart. He is not deceived by outward enthusiasm, nor shaken by the ups and downs of people's emotions.

Jesus' not entrusting Himself to emotional believers is for our good. He wants us to believe not because of the spectacle but because of the truth; not only to draw near when things go well but to lean on Him in hardship too. What He longs for is a simple, genuine heart willing to be ruled by Him, not a passing enthusiasm.

This passage also reminds us to ask: when we come before the Lord, are we only asking Him to do things and perform miracles? Or are we willing to let Him enter the deepest, truest places of our hearts? The Lord knows our motives, struggles, fears, pride, and weakness, and He knows what we need most. He is not rejecting us; He is leading us from surface belief into real belief, from the faith that sees miracles into the faith that knows Him.
q: Do you believe in the Lord because of what He has “done,” or because of who He “is”? Will you give the depths of your heart to Him, so that He may have complete rule?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for knowing our hearts and being willing to lead us from surface faith into real faith. Let our faith be built not on circumstances or feelings but on Your Word and Your truth. May our hearts be truly entrusted to You, and may You be King in our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.
The same came to him by night, and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.”
Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew,  he can’t see God’s Kingdom.”
b: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews, a man of high standing, deep knowledge, and upright conduct. He knew the Scriptures well, kept the law strictly, and was respected among the religious leaders. Yet deep inside he still felt an emptiness. He had seen Jesus' signs, seen people's praise, seen a reality he could not deny, and so he came seeking by night. His visit at night shows that he was struggling, but also that he was longing: he did not dare let people know, yet could not ignore his own need.

When he spoke he was very humble, calling Jesus “Rabbi” and acknowledging that His power came from God. Though Nicodemus held an honored position, he was willing to set aside his status and come to Jesus with respect and seeking. What the Lord saw was not only his knowledge but the longing in his heart: a longing to understand the truth, to enter the kingdom of God, and for life to be more than rules and form.

Jesus did not respond to his polite opening but cut straight to the core: “Unless one is born anew, he can’t see the Kingdom of God.” The Lord's words were like a light shining into Nicodemus's world, which he thought he already understood. Jesus pointed out a spiritual fact: human effort, status, background, knowledge, and religious performance cannot bring a person into the kingdom of God. Only new birth, being born of God and born from above, lets a person truly see the kingdom of God and truly know God.

New birth is not improving the old life but receiving a new life; not changing to a different set of behaviors but changing the source of life. A person cannot give himself new birth, just as a child cannot give himself birth; new birth is God's work, the Holy Spirit renewing us within, so that we no longer rely on ourselves but let the life of Christ come alive in us.
q: Is your pursuit of faith outward knowledge and behavior, or a life truly born of God? Will you let the Lord begin a new work in you, giving you new birth, renewal, and change?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for revealing the truth to us through Jesus. Let us not rely on our own effort or outward piety, but be truly born of You and renewed by You. May the Holy Spirit work within us, making us more and more like Your Son, living in Your kingdom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?”
Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’
The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”
b: Nicodemus still understood “new birth” from a physical point of view, so he was puzzled: how can an old man enter his mother's womb a second time? This exposes the limits of human beings: our natural life can only analyze with reason and cannot understand spiritual things. Jesus pointed out that new birth is not a second physical birth but a renewal of the source of life, a new life from God, a spiritual rebirth.

Jesus said, “Unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into the Kingdom of God.” “Water” represents cleansing and repentance, and “Spirit” represents the giving of life and renewal. New birth is not a religious ritual, nor merely the form of a prayer of decision, but the work the Holy Spirit does personally in a person's heart, bringing him from the old life into the new. What is born of the flesh can only live out the limits of the flesh; what is born of the Spirit can live a spiritual life, with heavenly values and God's perspective.

Jesus then used the wind as an illustration: “The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” The wind cannot be seen, but its power can be felt; the Spirit's work cannot be seen either, but it can change hearts. The wind brings movement, freshness, and renewal; the Spirit brings repentance, faith, obedience, and change. Where the wind has passed it leaves traces; where the Spirit touches it leaves the fruit of new life.

Jesus wanted Nicodemus to understand that spiritual life does not come from human effort but from the Spirit's work; not from piling up deeds but from a changed life; not from outward religion but from inward new birth. We can see the kingdom of God and enter it because we are born of the Spirit and the life of Christ begins to work within us.
q: What traces of “the wind passing through” have you seen in your life lately? Will you let the Holy Spirit move freely in your heart, so that you live out a new life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help us no longer to understand spiritual things in a fleshly way, but to open ourselves and let the Holy Spirit do His renewing work in our hearts. May we not rely on ourselves but let Your life come alive in us, so that we are truly born from above. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?”
Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things?
Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know, and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness.
If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?
b: Nicodemus's question again reveals his confusion: “How can these things be?” He was sincerely seeking, but he still faced spiritual truth with natural thinking. He knew the Scriptures well, taught the people, and held a high position, yet he had no concept of new birth. This reminds us that knowledge can make a person clever but cannot give new birth; religion can make a person devout but cannot bring him into the kingdom of God; only the revelation of the Holy Spirit lets a person truly understand the truth.

Jesus said to him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things?” This was not a rebuke but the disclosure of a fact: if the heart is bound by religious form, even a great deal of knowledge may leave us still not understanding spiritual reality. Nicodemus was familiar with Old Testament theory but did not know the reality of life; he could teach the law but did not know how to be born of the Spirit. This is the problem of many people too: knowing a great deal, yet not truly knowing God.

Jesus went on, “We speak that which we know... and you don’t receive our witness.” Everything Jesus said was not theory but what He had personally seen, experienced, and witnessed. He came from heaven, saw the Father, understood the truth, and brought life. What He spoke was not guesswork but revelation; not inference but fact. Yet if a person's heart is unwilling to be taught, he cannot receive it even when the truth is right before him.

The Lord said, “If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” “Earthly things” refers to new birth, God working in a person's heart to give new life, which still happens within a person. If Nicodemus found even this hard to accept, how much more the deeper mysteries of heaven. If a person does not first surrender and lay down himself, he cannot enter the spiritual realm or understand God's greater revelation.

In summary, Jesus wanted Nicodemus to understand that spiritual truth is received not through wisdom but through humility and faith; not through human reasoning but through the illumination of the Holy Spirit. Only when we are willing to admit our limits and let go of “what we already know” can we truly begin to “understand the things of God.”
q: Do you too often limit God's work by your own understanding? Today, will you adjust your heart and let the Lord teach you again, so that you learn to receive from the Holy Spirit?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give us humble hearts, so that we do not rely on our own knowledge but sincerely seek the Holy Spirit's revelation. Shine on us so that we may receive heavenly truth, no longer staying at head knowledge but truly entering the reality of life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.
As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up,
that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
b: Jesus reveals an extremely important truth to Nicodemus: no one can ascend into heaven by his own ability, effort, or religious achievement. Only the Son of Man, who came down from heaven, has heaven's authority and revelation. This shatters every illusion that we can approach God “on our own, by our works,” because only Jesus can bring heaven's truth to us and bring us back into God's presence.

He is not an earthly teacher but a Savior from heaven; He did not learn truth from men, He is the truth, the Word made flesh. What Nicodemus lacked was a revealed knowledge: we cannot climb up to God. We can only rely on the One who came down from heaven to bring us out of darkness into light.

Jesus then cites a story Nicodemus knew well: Moses lifting up the bronze serpent in the wilderness. The people, punished for their sin, had been bitten by fiery serpents, and all they had to do was look up at the lifted serpent to be healed and live (Numbers 21). This history foreshadows Jesus: He would be lifted up on the cross, bearing the sin of the world, so that all who look to Him would be healed, forgiven, and given life.
A person bitten by a snake in the wilderness cannot save himself; likewise, a person in sin cannot free himself by his own strength.

The way then was not to drink medicine, run away, or try to do good, but simply to “look up” at the serpent that was lifted up. Salvation today is likewise not by merit, performance, or religion, but by “looking to the crucified Jesus.”

This is the simplicity, clarity, and depth of the gospel: it is not about what we can do, but about what Jesus has already done for us. It is not saving ourselves by our own effort, but believing in His salvation.

Jesus says, “that whoever believes in him will have eternal life.” Eternal life is not something that happens only in the future; it begins the moment we believe, because eternal life is a restored relationship with God and entering into His life. It is not merely a ticket to heaven someday, but a life of fellowship with God, walking with Him and dwelling with Him today.
q: Are you still trying to “be saved” by your own efforts? Today, will you lay down your own methods and simply turn your eyes to the Savior who was lifted up for you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus down from heaven to open the way home for us. Help us no longer to depend on ourselves, but simply to look to Him and trust Him, so that we may live in the eternal life You give. May Your light shine on us, that we may deeply know salvation is not by works but by Your grace. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.
b: This passage is the heart of the whole Bible and the purest core of the gospel: God loves the world. Not because the world is lovable, nor because it deserves it, but because God's very nature is love. He loved to the point of giving His one and only Son. This is not an exchange or a transaction, but a complete, unreserved self-giving. Salvation is not man seeking God; it is God pursuing man, seeking man, loving man to the end.

The highest expression of God's love is that He gave us Jesus. Jesus did not come to teach a religious method or demand that people reach some standard; He came to be the way, so that we could return to the Father. He did not come to condemn but to save; not to judge but to restore. God is not a Lord enthroned on high waiting to judge people; He is a Savior who came down, entered our world, died for us, and rose for us.

Jesus says, “whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” Eternal life is not merely a future hope; it is a life we can experience now. To believe is not just to agree with the mind, but to open the heart to Him, to admit our limits, and to be willing to let Jesus reign in our hearts. This faith means we no longer perish, no longer stay cut off from God, no longer remain bound by sin, but enter a living relationship with God's presence.

“He who doesn't believe has been judged already” does not mean God is eager to condemn anyone; it points to a spiritual reality: if people reject the only Savior, they remain in a state of perishing. The problem of sin is not only “doing wrong,” but refusing the One who can save us from sin. Those who reject the light remain in darkness; those who reject life remain in death; those who reject salvation remain in perishing. God does not push anyone toward destruction; people refuse the hand He holds out.
This is the truth of love: He gave the best, He paid the price, He opened the way, He calls us, He waits for us. If we are willing to believe, we receive eternal life, hope, and a new life.
q: Do you believe God loves you this much? Today, will you open your heart again, simply respond to this love, and let His life come alive in you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for loving us so much that You gave Your one and only Son. Help us no longer to rely on ourselves, but to trust in You alone. Let us live in the eternal life You give, free from fear, condemnation, and separation. May Your love renew our hearts every day, so that we truly live in Your presence. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil.
For everyone who does evil hates the light, and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed.
But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”
b: Jesus explains the real reason people reject Him: not that they cannot see the light, but that they do not love the light. Light represents truth, life, and holiness, and also God's call to us. Yet when the heart is bound by sin, self, pride, or fear, it flees from the light, because light exposes the truth people do not want to face. It is not that the light is too bright, but that the heart is unwilling to let the light in.

“Men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil.” The deepest power of sin lies not in behavior but in “loving the darkness.” Darkness gives the illusion that we need not face anything, admit anything, change anything, or give up control. Darkness feels safe, but it is only a prison for escaping the light.

“Everyone who does evil hates the light… lest his works would be exposed.” We hate the light not because the light is bad, but because it leaves us no way to deceive ourselves anymore. The light shows the truth, shows the old self, shows a life full of self, shows the control we are unwilling to surrender deep inside. So people flee the light, not because it hurts, but because they do not want to be renewed.

But Jesus goes on: “He who does the truth comes to the light.” “Doing the truth” does not mean being perfect; it means having a real and willing heart, willing to be illuminated, willing to be renewed, willing to let God be in charge.

Such a person “comes to the light,” because he knows the light is not there to destroy him but to save him; not to expose his shame but to heal and restore him; not to condemn him but to bring him out of the darkness back into God's arms.

Jesus says, “that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.” When a person is willing to come into the light, his life is naturally changed by God: no longer by self but by God; no longer by strength but by grace; no longer by analysis but by the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
The light is not there to condemn but to make us live; not to catch our problems but to make us new selves; not to expose but to rebuild.
q: Are there places in your life where you still dare not let the light in? Today, will you come to the light with a real heart so that God can bring you healing and renewal?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help us no longer to flee the light, but to come boldly into it. Let us know that the light is not there to hurt us but to heal and renew us. Shine on the places in our lives that are still in darkness, so that we will be willing to let Jesus be King and walk every step by You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: After these things, Jesus came with his disciples into the land of Judea. He stayed there with them and baptized.
John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came, and were baptized;
for John was not yet thrown into prison.
b: In this passage we see a quiet but spiritually significant scene: Jesus and John baptizing at the same time. Two ministries run side by side, with no competition, no comparison, and no jealousy. It is one of the rare pictures of spiritual leaders with “no separation and no opposition.” Both knew their place before God, and both kept their focus on God's will rather than on their own reputation.

Jesus' ministry was just beginning to flourish and His disciples were increasing; John's ministry was drawing to a close, and he knew he “must decrease.” Yet he kept on serving faithfully, still baptizing and still leading people to repentance, until the moment God told him to stop. He did not rush to grasp power or fear being replaced; with the humblest attitude he fulfilled the role God had given him.

This passage also shows us an important principle: true ministry that belongs to God completes one another rather than competing. When people compare, relationships break; when people long to be seen, separation arises; but when the focus is on God, each person can be faithful in his own place, supplementing rather than crowding out one another.

John chose to baptize at Aenon “because there was much water there.” This reminds us of a spiritual wisdom: God's work needs “water,” a symbol of the Spirit's supply and presence. Without God's presence, no amount of method helps; but with water, with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, God's work flourishes naturally rather than being propped up by human effort.

The passage ends: “For John had not yet been thrown into prison.” This line seems plain, but it is a foreshadowing. John's ministry on earth would end, yet God's plan did not stop. God uses a person for a season, but His kingdom does not stop because one person leaves the stage. This reminds us that we are vessels, not the center; God's kingdom is eternal, and we are only workers in it.
q: In your service or daily life, have you ever lost peace through comparison? Today, what does God want you to lay down so that you can be faithful and joyful in your place?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, make us like Jesus and John, with hearts of humility and obedience in service. Let us not compare or compete, but be willing to stand in the place You gave us and faithfully complete what You entrusted to us. May everything we do bear fruit because of the abundant water of the Holy Spirit, not because of our own effort. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Therefore a dispute arose on the part of John’s disciples with some Jews about purification.
They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.”
John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
b: This passage presents a scene common to human nature: comparison, competition, and insecurity. John's disciples saw Jesus' ministry flourishing, with everyone going to Him, and became anxious, even complaining uneasily to John. What concerned them was “who has more followers,” “whose momentum is greater,” “whose influence is stronger.” This is exactly the trap the human heart easily falls into: treating ministry as our own achievement rather than God's work.

But John's answer shows deep spiritual wisdom. He says, “A man can receive nothing, unless it has been given him from heaven.” That is, every true gift, opportunity, identity, and fruit comes from God; it is not won by our striving or by comparison. What God gives, we cannot lose; what God does not give, we cannot grab. When we understand that everything comes from God, the heart stops clutching, stops striving, stops comparing, and rests in God's will.

John reminds the disciples, “I am not the Christ.” He knows his role: the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom. Ministry is not about building “our own name,” but about preparing the way for people to know Jesus. When people are brought to the Lord, John is not disappointed but joyful. This is a truly self-denied life: stepping back so that Christ can be seen in front.

He says, “The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice. Therefore my joy is made full.” The bridegroom has come and the bride is drawn to him; John is not jealous but glad. When Christ works and rises up in someone's life, that is the greatest joy, and even if we step down and stay hidden, we are satisfied, because the focus is not ourselves but the glory of the bridegroom.

The final sentence is the peak of the whole passage and the mark of a mature spiritual life: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” This does not mean ministry will bear no fruit from now on; it means that what people see, follow, and rely on should not be me but Jesus. My role was never the center; the purpose of my existence is to lift Him up.

When we are willing to “decrease,” Jesus “increases” in us; when we stop grabbing control, He can reign in our lives; when self steps down and Christ takes the throne, life glorifies God and bears eternal fruit.
q: In the relationships and ministry you face now, where do you most need to say, “Lord, let You increase and let me decrease”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, put a heart like John's in us, so that we no longer compare, no longer grasp, no longer care about our position, but long only to see Jesus lifted up. May we say in everything, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Let You receive the glory, and let us receive true peace and joy. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all.
What he has seen and heard, of that he testifies; and no one receives his witness.
He who has received his witness has set his seal to this, that God is true.
b: John continues here to testify to Jesus' identity, helping people understand why he said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” For Jesus is not an ordinary teacher, prophet, or spiritual leader; He is the One who “comes from above,” the Lord who came down from heaven and is above all.

“He who is from the earth belongs to the earth.” No matter how wise, gifted, or powerful a person is, he is still limited, still earthly, still bound by limits. No matter how deep a person's insight, it cannot reach the complete truth of heaven. An earthly view always sees fragments rather than the whole; an earthly voice always brings limited help rather than complete life.

But Jesus is different. He comes from heaven, and what He brings is not speculation but revelation; not doctrine but truth; not human philosophy but God's heart. Everything He says comes from what “He has seen and heard”; He came from heaven, so He can testify to heavenly things.

Yet the text says, “No one receives his witness.” It is not because He spoke unclearly or His words were hard to understand, but because the human heart is often unwilling to submit. People would rather hold on to their own views than accept the light from heaven; rather protect their own positions than let truth shine; rather rely on their own analysis than trust with the heart.

But “He who has received his witness has set his seal to this, that God is true.” That is, whoever is willing to receive and believe what Jesus says has personally verified that God is real and trustworthy. This is not proof in the mind but a mark deep in life. When a person gives his heart to the Lord, gives control to the Lord, and places his faith in Him, he experiences His faithfulness, guidance, presence, and work, and so knows deeply: “God is true.”
In other words, faith is like setting a seal: when we receive Jesus' words, we put a seal on our lives that testifies, “I believe God, I believe His word, I believe He is real.”
q: Have you recently replaced God's revelation with your own analysis? In what matter do you need to receive Jesus' testimony afresh and set that seal in your heart: God is true?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus down from heaven to bring truth, light, and life to us. Give us a willing heart to receive, so that we rely not on our own understanding but sincerely believe Your testimony. May Your truth be engraved on our hearts like a seal, so that every day we live out a life that says, “God is true.” In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure.
The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.
One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys  the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”
b: This passage is the peak of the whole third chapter, again bringing together Christ's identity, the work of the Spirit, the Father's love, and the truth of eternal life. Here it is not John's lofty rhetoric but the deepest revelation about Jesus that the Holy Spirit speaks through him.

“For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God.” What Jesus says are not human words, philosophy, or dogma, but the word of life from the Father. Every sentence He speaks carries the weight of truth, the light of eternity, and the renewal of life. When He speaks, people are not listening to a teacher but to the Heavenly Father speaking to them.

“For God gives the Spirit without measure.” People have limits, but the Spirit in Jesus is limitless. Human gifts, wisdom, power, and love are limited; but the Spirit given to Jesus is complete, full, overflowing, and without bounds. His miracles, compassion, wisdom, and forgiveness are not human power but come from the boundless outpouring of the Spirit within Him.

“The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.” The Father has given everything to Jesus: time, eternity, life, judgment, authority, salvation, kingdom, and future. He is Lord of all, the center of history, the ruler of heaven and earth. This world is not chaos or chance; it is in Christ's hands. If we look only at circumstances, we will be afraid; but when we see that all things are in His hands, we can be at ease, rest, and have peace.

The last sentence brings the whole message to the core of personal life: “One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won't see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.” Eternal life is not only for the future; it is given now to all who believe. To believe is to enter life; not to believe is to remain in death. To believe is to receive the light; not to believe is to stay in darkness. To believe is to let Jesus be King; not to believe is to keep ruling oneself.

“The wrath of God remains on him” is not an emotion but a spiritual reality: those who reject life can only live in death; those who reject light can only live in darkness; those who reject salvation can only bear the consequences of sin. God does not want anyone to perish; people themselves reject the only Savior.

And those who are willing to believe have eternal life immediately: a restored relationship with God, a new life beginning to work within, true light illuminating life's direction, the Holy Spirit dwelling in the heart as guide, and Christ's love becoming the strength of life.
q: Today, are you living by “self in control,” or by “Jesus in control”? In what matter are you willing to say again, “Lord, I trust You, and I place all this in Your hands”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for placing all things in Jesus' hands and giving eternal life to all who believe in Him. Help us trust Him deeply, obey Him, and rely on His word, letting Him reign in our lives, so that we live in the power of eternal life. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Therefore when the Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John
(although Jesus himself didn’t baptize, but his disciples),
he left Judea and departed into Galilee.
b: This short passage seems only to record a change in Jesus' itinerary, yet it holds deep spiritual wisdom, showing the Lord's heart, His gentleness and humility, His complete obedience to the Father's will, and His unwillingness to stir up unnecessary strife.

When the Pharisees heard that Jesus' influence was growing and His disciples were multiplying, their jealousy, hostility, and sense of threat rose. This tension had only begun to ferment, and Jesus did not choose confrontation, nor did He use the momentum to build Himself up, nor did He meet the religious leaders head-on.
He chose to leave quietly.

Not because He was afraid, nor because He shrank back, but because He knew the time had not yet come. His whole life was in complete obedience to the Father's timing and the Father's plan, neither early nor late. He did not let conflict lead His steps, nor let people's jealousy decide His route. He made no decision to “please the crowd” and took no action to “prove Himself”; He simply moved forward according to the Heavenly Father's will.
This also teaches us a vital spiritual lesson: not every conflict needs to be confronted head-on, and not every challenge needs us to prove ourselves.
Sometimes the most spiritual response is not to counterattack but to “leave.” Not to escape, but to keep unnecessary tension from blocking God's greater work.

Jesus left because He knew the real battlefield was the cross, not religious arguments; He knew His mission was to accomplish salvation, not to argue over who was more spiritual or whose disciples were more numerous. He kept His focus on the Heavenly Father, not on people's eyes.

Verse 2 specifically says: “(although Jesus himself didn't baptize, but his disciples).” This shows the Lord's humility and delegation. He did not seize credit or fight for fame, nor did He concentrate the ministry in His own hands. He gladly let the disciples take part and be built up in the work. He did not place Himself at center stage or need to stand out as the only worker, because everything He did was for the glory of the Father, not to build a personal reputation.

Let us consider: if one day your ministry is compared, your position questioned, and your influence noticed, will you, like Jesus, stay gentle, simple, quiet, and self-denied? Will you refuse to compete, refuse to rush to explain or prove yourself, and simply follow God's leading?
q: Recently, has something in your life made you want to “prove yourself”?
Today, is the Lord inviting you to walk the path He has prepared for you in a gentler, quieter, more obedient way?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, teach us to be like Jesus, not led along by people's eyes, comparison, jealousy, or conflict, but simply following Your guidance. Give us a humble heart that does not hurry to prove itself but is willing to step back, so that You are first in our lives. May You lead us to live out self-denial at every step, so that everything glorifies You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: He needed to pass through Samaria.
So he came to a city of Samaria, called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son, Joseph.
Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being tired from his journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour.
b: These verses look like an ordinary travel record but hide a deep purpose of God. The text says, “He needed to pass through Samaria.” For the Jews, “passing through Samaria” was never necessary; it was a road they deliberately avoided. Going from Judea to Galilee, Jews usually detoured east of the Jordan, just to avoid contact with Samaritans, whom they considered “unclean,” “impure,” and “unworthy.”

But Jesus chose the road people avoided. He walked into places people thought He should not go, drew near to people they thought unworthy, and entered realms they regarded as dark, mixed, and shameful.

He said He “needed” to pass through, not out of geographical necessity but out of the Heavenly Father's heart. He needed to enter a rejected people. He needed to wait for a broken woman. He needed to keep an appointment of salvation. He needed to restore a heart abandoned by the world.

Jesus came to Sychar and sat by Jacob's well. The words “being tired from his journey” show His gentleness and humanity. The eternal God was willing to put on a weary body; the Lord who created the universe walked the roads of life Himself, experiencing human hardship, thirst, and limitation.
He sat by the well at “about the sixth hour,” the hottest time of day, when people are least likely to draw water, and exactly when the Samaritan woman deliberately avoided the crowds.

Jesus was not sitting there by chance; by the Heavenly Father's arrangement He sat where she would pass. He chose to wait for her there in her loneliest, quietest, most ashamed, least-wanting-to-be-seen moment.

This is how the Lord deals with everyone: He often sits waiting for us in the place we least want to face; He often appears when we think life is most dried up; He often prepares a moment of restoration behind our hiding from people; He often walks into the inner corners we avoid, bringing light into darkness, love into shame, and grace into the places where we feel unworthy.

The text begins, “He needed to pass through Samaria.” In fact, He “needed to pass through the Samaria of your heart.” The places you dare not face, your shameful past, your broken relationships, your hidden wounds are where He wants to go. He never despises and never detours; He comes toward you.
q: Is there also a “Samaria” in your heart, a place you have kept avoiding and are unwilling to face?
Today, will you let Jesus pass through there, sit down, and wait to meet you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your love does not detour, and that You are willing to walk into our most broken and shameful places. Sit today at the well of our lives, so that we may meet You, hear You, and drink the living water of life. Let us be willing to open our hearts and let You walk into the corners we dare not face, so that we receive healing and restoration. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.
The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
b: This passage portrays a profound, gentle, and revolutionary scene: the eternal God takes the initiative to speak to a broken, lonely, rejected woman entangled in many troubles.
The disciples were absent, leaving only Jesus and her. It was a carefully arranged encounter, free from interruption, solely to touch a lonely heart.

That the woman came to draw water at “the sixth hour” itself reveals her shame and isolation. Normal women drew water in groups in the early morning and evening; only she did not want to meet anyone or be seen by anyone. She avoided everyone, yet met the Lord who was seeking her.

Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” He chose to open the conversation in the simplest, most ordinary, least threatening way. He did not accuse, expose, rebuke, or lecture her, but simply said, “Give me a drink.” By asking her for something, He respected her, lifted her up, and gave her worth, letting her know she had something to give rather than being unworthy of everything.
This one sentence took down the wall in her heart.

Yet she was still astonished: “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” One sentence expresses her lifelong inferiority: ethnic barrier, “I am a Samaritan”; gender barrier, “I am a woman”; status barrier, “I am a woman with a problem”; moral barrier, “I don't deserve to be noticed by you”; spiritual barrier, “I have no right for you to speak to me.”

Her astonishment was because she had never been taken seriously by a Jewish man, especially a Jewish rabbi like Jesus. But Jesus did not detour, discriminate, shrink back, or pick and choose whom He met. He crossed all the cultural taboos of the time just to touch a deeply broken heart.

“For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.” This sentence points to the deep hatred of that time, but Jesus chose to break through it all, because what He wants is people's hearts, not people's categories.

And His way was not to do something great, perform a miracle, or preach, but first to open her heart with a gentle request. He approached her not by shock but by gentleness; He healed her not by authority but by genuine acceptance.
This is Jesus: He is willing to wait in the hottest hour for the coldest heart, to approach the lowliest person in the humblest way, and to begin a conversation not to teach but to restore.
q: Are there places in your life where you think you are “unworthy to be touched by God”?
Today, will you, like this woman, let Jesus speak to you in that place?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your love is always initiating, gentle, and never detouring. Open our hearts so that we are willing to let You draw near to the most shameful places in our lives, and teach us, like Jesus, to reach out with gentleness to those in need. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. So where do you get that living water?
Are you greater than our father, Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his children and his livestock?”
b: Jesus reveals to the woman the deepest truth about life, saying, “If you knew the gift of God…” The problem is not that she was not thirsty, but that she did not know what she truly needed; not that she did not want water, but that she did not know there is a “living water” that can truly satisfy her heart.

If she had known who stood before her, not a passing Jewish man, not a stranger breaking cultural taboos, but the gift sent from God, the source of life, she would not have responded passively but would have sought Him eagerly. Jesus said, “You would have asked him.” He meant: “If you knew what He could give you, you would not stay on your guard, but would long for Him.”

All her life this woman had craved love, acceptance, and security. She had tried to fill the thirst in her heart with five broken marriages, but the more she drank the drier she became, and the more she searched the emptier she felt. Jesus knew her inner thirst and knew she had been drinking “well water,” the substitutes that cannot truly satisfy the soul.

Yet the woman stayed on “visible needs.” She replied, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep…” It is as if she were saying, “By what right can you give? How could you do it? What power do you have?”

Her thinking was limited to material things, tools, and circumstances, but the “living water” Jesus spoke of does not come from a well but from God. She saw “no bucket”; Jesus saw that she “had no life.”

She went further: “Are you greater than our father, Jacob?” This question reveals that her heart still clung to tradition, background, ancestors, and custom. She placed Jesus in a position of comparison, as people often treat faith as one option among many.
But Jesus is not “a better option”; He is the only source of life. He is not someone to be compared with Jacob; He is Jacob's Lord. He is not the owner of a well; He is the fountain of living water.
Jesus gently led her to turn her eyes from well water to living water, from the bucket to grace, from the problem to the Savior, from historical tradition to the truth of eternal life.
He was telling her, “What you really thirst for is not well water but love; not a man but grace; not circumstances but life; not tools but a Savior.”
q: What “well water” have you been using to prop yourself up?
Today, will you turn to Jesus and ask Him for the living water that truly satisfies the soul?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help us to know Your gift, Jesus Christ. Open our eyes so that we no longer fix our focus on outward conditions or human methods, but return to You, the source of life. Let our hearts truly long for You, seek You, and drink the living water You give. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”
b: Jesus' answer is very direct and profound. He points out two completely different waters, two completely different sources of life, and two completely different outcomes.

“Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again.” “This water” means the water of Jacob's well, and also symbolizes all the “substitutes” people find for themselves in the world: things that seem to satisfy briefly but can never resolve the thirst deep in the soul. These include:
• Relationships (like this woman's search for one romantic relationship after another)
• Achievement and success
• Wealth and security
• Human approval
• Pleasure and entertainment
• Religious ritual
• Our own methods and willpower
All of these can bring temporary comfort but cannot truly satisfy. After drinking we thirst again; after gaining we are empty again; the more we chase, the more tired we become.

Jesus is not criticizing the well water as bad, but pointing out its limited power: it can satisfy the body but not the heart. The water of this world can never reach the soul, so after drinking we still thirst.

“Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty.” Jesus does not give a better well but gives “Himself.” The water He gives is His life, His love, His presence, His salvation, His light, His truth. What He can quench is “heart thirst,” not “mouth thirst.”
True thirst is not a lack in our circumstances but a lack of life; true hunger and thirst is not a shortage of material things but a soul without a source.
Having drunk His living water, the heart no longer needs to search aimlessly, cling to people, lean on circumstances, or chase the things that leave people drier and drier.
Jesus adds, “The water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.” What He gives is not a bucket of water, not a well, but “a spring within.”
This spring has several characteristics:
First, it is internal, not added from outside.
It does not depend on circumstances, other people, or emotions, but on the Holy Spirit flowing from within.
Second, it is continuous, not temporary.
It is not inspired today and dried up tomorrow; it is not sustained by a momentary spiritual high, but the Holy Spirit keeps welling up with new life.
Third, it leads to eternal life.
It gives not only strength for this life but brings us into an eternal connection with God.

True satisfaction does not come from outside but from within; true rest does not come from circumstances but from the Holy Spirit; true life does not come from effort but from the living water Jesus gives.
q: Are you still drinking the waters that leave you thirsty again?
Today, will you ask Jesus to put the living water within you, so that you no longer depend on outside sources, but a spring of eternal life wells up in your heart?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving us Your life, so that we no longer drink the well water of the world but Your living water. Let the Holy Spirit flow within us, so that we no longer lean on things that leave us drier and drier, but depend on You every day and are satisfied in You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw.”
Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”
The woman answered, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You said well, ‘I have no husband,’
for you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have is not your husband. This you have said truly.”
b: When the woman heard of the living water Jesus gives, which means “never thirsty again,” she immediately said, “Sir, give me this water.” Her words seem to show longing, but they stay at a surface need: “that I don't get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw.” She wanted convenience, ease, and less hardship, while Jesus wanted to give her healing and renewal at the depth of life.
Many people are like her, hoping faith will relieve stress, smooth things out, and make life easier, rather than letting Jesus truly touch the deepest need of their hearts.

So Jesus gently but directly cut to the core of her life: “Go, call your husband, and come here.” He was not exposing her sores but leading her into reality. For true healing is not avoidance but being exposed in love; true satisfaction is not switching methods but changing life.
The woman answered, “I have no husband.” It was half the truth, spoken with self-protection; she did not want to bring up her past, her brokenness, and her shame.

Jesus said, “You said well.” He then gently and clearly described her situation: “For you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have is not your husband.” Jesus knew all her past, her tears, failures, pain, and loneliness, but He did not shame her or judge her. With truth He pointed to her deepest thirst, and with love He covered her deepest pain.
He did not want her to bear shame but to lead her out of shame. He did not want her to bear blame but to lead her into freedom. He did not open her wound to hurt her; He opened her wound to heal it.

Here Jesus shows us a spiritual principle: before He puts living water within us, He first touches the part we avoid. Not to sting but to heal at the root; not to expose but to restore; not to accuse but to renew.
This woman kept escaping crowds, relationships, and her past, but she could not escape the thirst in her heart. Jesus touched her deepest wound precisely to pour living water into her driest place.
q: Do you also have a past and wounds you are unwilling to let God touch?
Today, will you trust His love and let Him speak and bring healing in that place?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for touching our reality with love. Help us no longer to hide, no longer to protect ourselves with half-truths, but to be willing to let You open the wounds deep within us so that You Yourself can heal them. May Your living water flow into our driest hearts, so that we receive true release and renewal. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.
Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”
b: After Jesus gently and truthfully touched the wound in the woman's life, she immediately changed the subject. She jumped from a relationship problem to a theological issue, from personal life to religious debate. This is an extremely common human reaction: when the truth is too painful, too close, too deep, we want to shift the focus, talking about theory, doctrine, and institutions, as if talking about spiritual things could avoid the real question in our hearts.

The woman said, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.” On the surface this was respect, but in fact it was a way of “keeping distance”: she did not deny Jesus' insight, yet she did not want Him to go any deeper into her life. She acknowledged that He had the word of God, yet still would not hand over the deepest part of her heart.
So she raised a theological question Jews and Samaritans had long argued about: “Where should people worship?” Mount Gerizim? Jerusalem? She thought changing to a spiritual topic would make her safe.
But her question reveals three things:
First, she actually longed to know the truth.
She was not deliberately twisting right and wrong; she had been crushed by the burdens of life for so long, and in her heart she really wanted to know, “Where can I truly meet God?”
Second, she thought worship was determined by “place.”
Religion often makes people think that going to the right place, doing the right rituals, and keeping the right rules will satisfy God.
Third, she wanted to cover the emptiness in her life with an emphasis on form.
Discussing “where to worship” is much easier than facing “whether my heart is willing to worship.”
Yet Jesus did not come to argue with her about the “mountain” and the “city”; He came to lead her into true worship: not a place but the heart; not form but truth; not ritual but life.
Jesus tore down all religious boundaries, because salvation is not reserved for people in “a certain place” but for those who are “willing to seek Him with the heart.”
The woman wanted to change the subject, but Jesus wanted to turn back to her heart. He did not come to answer religious questions; He came to save a broken soul.
He did not come to let her know where to worship; He came to make her a true worshiper.
q: When the Lord touches the depths of your life, do you also often use “busyness,” “theory,” or “ministry” to shift the focus?
Today, will you stop and bring your heart back to Him in truth?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help us not to cover our hearts with theory, knowledge, or a religious shell, but to be willing to face You in truth. Lead us from pursuing form into real worship, from avoiding the truth into Your love and light. May our hearts return to You, and may You be the focus of our worship. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour comes, when neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, will you worship the Father.
You worship that which you don’t know. We worship that which we know; for salvation is from the Jews.
But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”
b: Jesus did not respond to the woman's evasive topic or fall into religious debate; He pointed directly to the core truth of worship, bringing a shamed and broken woman into the deepest revelation of worship in the whole Bible: true worship is not on a mountain, nor in Jerusalem, but in the depths of the heart.

He first said, “Woman, believe me.” He was not discussing a theological issue but calling her to trust Him. He meant: “Stop evading, stop covering the need of your soul with intellectual questions, and simply trust Me.” True worship is not a place but a relationship, a relationship of trust.

Jesus then said, “The hour comes, when neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem…” He tore down the geographical boundaries of religion. Salvation is not reserved for people in one region but for all who are willing to open their hearts.
Worship is not in some holy place but anywhere a person is willing to open up to God.
This sentence proclaims a revolutionary truth: worship is not moving the feet but moving the heart; not an outward ritual but an inner life.
Jesus went on, “You worship that which you don't know.” The Samaritan religion the woman represented was a mixed, vague, traditional worship, with form but without true knowledge.

“We worship that which we know” points out that salvation is from the Jews, because God revealed Himself in Jewish history, sent His Son, and fulfilled the promise of salvation. Yet Jesus was not stressing ethnic superiority, but saying that true knowing comes not through tradition but through revelation.

Then He spoke the core of worship: “The true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” “Spirit” is not emotional excitement but the depth of a person, where we are real, free, and meet God. “Truth” means fellowship with God with nothing hidden, and worshiping according to the truth God has revealed.
This worship is not acting, not form, not deliberately putting on a spiritual appearance, but truly bringing ourselves before God, letting Him see, touch, renew, and guide.

The last sentence: “For the Father seeks such to be his worshippers.” God does not demand a particular way of worship; He seeks “people”: people who are real in heart; people whose hearts are surrendered; people whose hearts have no separation; people whose hearts are open to Him.
He does not want a religious performance; He wants children who draw near to Him. He does not want empty ritual; He wants a living connection.
He does not want us to come wearing masks; He wants us to come as we really are.
This woman never knew she could worship, but Jesus told her, “The Father is looking for you.”
q: Is your worship today formal, intellectual, or real and open?
What corner of your life do you need to bring to Him so that He can touch it, and you can truly worship Him in spirit and truth?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You do not demand that we do something, but long for our hearts to return to You. Teach us to worship You in spirit and truth, without hiding, pretending, or mixing, but meeting You in reality. May our worship not be form but life. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.”
Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”
b: This moment is the climax of the whole encounter and the beginning of this woman's complete turnaround. From avoiding the issue, to facing the truth, to being illuminated, to longing to know the truth, she finally voiced the deepest hope of her heart:
“I know that Messiah comes… when he has come, he will declare to us all things.”
This sentence reveals three important attitudes:
First, in her heart she had always longed for a true Savior.

Although her life was broken and a mess; although she had no spiritual background and no good image; although she was rejected by others and denied by herself; deep inside she still kept a thread of hope that one day the true Savior would come and tell her how to walk out of the darkness.
She thought she was looking for water; Jesus knew she was looking for salvation.
Second, she actually longed for truth, but had no outlet.
She knew the religion she had heard was confused and unclear; she wanted to know the truth but did not know where to find it; she wanted to meet God but thought she was unworthy.
Yet she was willing to say it aloud: “The Christ is coming.” This was a spark of faith in her heart, faint but still burning.
Third, she acknowledged that only the Messiah could answer life's real questions.
She said, “He will declare to us all things.” She meant: “Only He can show the direction, only He can bring out the truth, only He can answer the confusion of my life.”
Her heart was being prepared and led to the most important moment.
Just then, Jesus spoke the most startling, direct, and gentle revelation of the whole passage:
“I am he, the one who speaks to you.”
This was not a public declaration to the crowds, not a loud teaching in the synagogue, not an argument with religious leaders, but a gentle revelation to a broken, lonely, ashamed woman.
For the first time the Messiah directly announced His identity, not to Nicodemus, not to the chief priests, not to the scribes, but to this overlooked Samaritan woman.
Because God's seeking often does not begin with the most impressive people but with the most broken.
Jesus seemed to say to her, “The One you have been waiting for, the One your heart longs for, the Savior you thought would never come to you, is Me.”

He made the whole journey just to sit by the well and wait for her; He passed through every prejudice just to let her know she was loved; He crossed spiritual and cultural boundaries just to say this one sentence: “I am your Savior.”
q: What is Jesus saying to you?
Will you believe that “the One speaking to me is He”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your love is so personal, so gentle, and so real. You see the longing deep in each of us and are willing to reveal Yourself to us personally. Help us, like this woman, no longer to evade or hide, but to open our hearts and recognize the Lord who speaks to us. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: At this, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?”
So the woman left her water pot, went away into the city, and said to the people,
“Come, see a man who told me everything that I did. Can this be the Christ?”
