They went out of the city, and were coming to him.
b: When Jesus revealed His true identity to the Samaritan woman, the disciples suddenly returned. They saw Jesus talking with a Samaritan woman and “marveled.” In that culture a rabbi would not speak publicly with a woman, much less a Samaritan woman. But the disciples' surprise reflects one thing: Jesus' love often breaks through limits people cannot see.

Though surprised, the disciples did not dare ask, because Jesus' actions often went beyond their understanding. While people were still dividing along “boundaries” and “peoples,” Jesus was already looking at a heart that needed to be loved.
Then the scene turns to the woman, who did something crucial, beautiful, and symbolic:
“So the woman left her water pot.”

She had come to the well to draw water; when she left, the true water was already welling up in her heart. What she left by the well was not only a vessel but the way she had used to hold herself up. That water pot was a symbol of how she barely got through each day.
But when Jesus became her fountain of life, that pot no longer mattered.
She left what she had thought most important and ran toward a mission she had never had.

She went straight into the city, the city she had not wanted to face, among the people she had wanted to avoid. In the past she hid from people, avoided people, feared meeting people; now she appeared among the crowd without fear.
Love makes us stop hiding. Those who have been seen by Jesus can also boldly be seen by the world.
She said to the people, “Come, see a man who told me everything that I did.” She was no longer afraid of her past, because she had met a grace greater than her past.

She even raised a possibility that shook everyone: “Can this be the Christ?” She who had been too ashamed to speak became a missionary to a whole city. She who had avoided people now dared to bring people to Jesus.
The whole city began to move: “They went out of the city, and were coming to him.”
A despised woman became the gate of blessing that led people to Jesus. This is Jesus' way: He often chooses the most broken to accomplish the greatest and most beautiful testimony.
She had no sermon, no theology, no strategy; she had only one thing: “Jesus saw me, and I have been changed by Him.”
True testimony is not technique but the life that flows naturally after being renewed by Jesus.
q: Are you still holding on to an “old water pot,” something you think keeps you alive?
Today, will you put it down and turn to run toward the new life and new mission God has for you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your love lets us stop hiding. May Your living water keep flowing, so that we put down the old pots we once clung to and run toward the new life You have entrusted to us. Use us, every day, to be a channel for others to meet Jesus. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: In the meanwhile, the disciples urged him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”
But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.”
The disciples therefore said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”
Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.
b: This passage turns from the woman running into the city to proclaim Jesus back to the conversation between Jesus and the disciples by the well. When the disciples returned, they began to care about the Lord's meal, saying, “Rabbi, eat.” In their eyes this was the most natural and practical need. But Jesus shifted their focus from “food” to “mission.”

Jesus answered, “I have food to eat that you don't know about.” He was not refusing to eat, but revealing a deeper principle of life: His life was sustained not by earthly provision but by the Heavenly Father's will.

The disciples still thought from a human angle: “Has anyone brought him something to eat?” Their reaction shows that when people do not understand spiritual reality, even following the Lord they may still stay at “surface needs.” They thought Jesus' satisfaction was outward, material, and visible, but His satisfaction was deep, spiritual, and invisible.
So Jesus uncovered the core secret of His life:
“My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work.”
He did not deny food, but said: my real source of strength, my real satisfaction, my real joy come not from eating and drinking but from doing the Father's will.
This is Jesus' pattern of life and His daily rhythm:
Not relying on Himself but only on the Heavenly Father; not doing His own work but only the Father's work; not seeking His own satisfaction but only the Father's pleasure.
His heart was fully aligned with the Father, His focus fully on the Father, His strength fully from the Father.

Here Jesus teaches the disciples, and us, an important spiritual truth: true joy comes from obeying the Heavenly Father. True strength comes from walking in His will. True satisfaction comes from completing the work God has entrusted.
Many feel that serving God makes them tired and worn out, but for Jesus, service was His “food,” the source of His daily renewal, strength, and satisfaction.
When He finished what the Heavenly Father asked Him to do, it was like someone who had eaten his fill: the heart satisfied, the spirit strengthened.
Jesus did not live by emotions, by circumstances, or by other people's support, but by the Heavenly Father's will.
q: What is the “real food” in your life?
Will you, like Jesus, make “doing the Father's will” your daily source of strength?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give us the life of Jesus, so that we no longer pursue only outward satisfaction but long to walk in Your will. May our food be doing Your will and accomplishing Your work in our lives. May our hearts, every day, find the source of joy in Your will. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest?’ Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.
He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit to eternal life; that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.
For in this the saying is true, ‘One sows, and another reaps.’
I sent you to reap that for which you haven’t labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”
b: By the well Jesus opened the disciples' eyes to the “time” as He saw it: not four months away, but “now.” He wanted the disciples to see what God was doing, rather than staying in the timetable they imagined.

He said, “Don't you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest’?” This reflects the habitual human way of thinking: wait a bit longer; the time hasn't come; not ready yet; we'll talk about it later.
But the Lord said, “Lift up your eyes, and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.”
That is: what you think is far away is right before you. What you think hasn't begun is already ripe. What you think needs more preparation, God is already at work.

Jesus let the disciples see the “Heavenly Father's perspective”: the woman had only just left, and people from a whole city were walking this way. The disciples saw only Jesus talking with a woman, but Jesus saw the beginning of a revival.
True harvest is not arranged by people but comes when God's prepared time arrives.

Then He said, “He who reaps receives wages, and gathers fruit to eternal life.” The “wages” here are not earthly pay but heavenly joy and eternal fruit. The harvester receives more than he gives: satisfaction from heaven, imperishable eternal fruit, and the glory of working with God.

He also said, “That both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.” In God's kingdom there is no comparison, no competition, no who-has-more, only the same joy, because every step is under God's control.
One sows, another waters, another tills, another reaps, but the glory belongs to the same God.

Jesus also said, “For in this the saying is true, ‘One sows, and another reaps.’” That you and I can reap today is because those before us sowed with tears; that someone's heart soil is prepared today is because someone prayed, gave, and walked with them. What we enter is not our own merit but God's long work.
Finally He said something extremely important: “I sent you to reap that for which you have not labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”
This sentence has three layers:
First, everyone stands on the foundation of those before.
The work of the gospel is not the achievement of one person but a relay across generations.
Second, the commission God gives the disciples is not pressure but grace.
Because God has already done most of it, and they simply join His work.
Third, a true worker looks at “what God has already done,” not “what I have not yet done.”
The focus is not whether we have the ability, but that God has already prepared the harvest field.
Jesus wanted the disciples to see that the woman He had just met had already drawn a whole city to harvest, and the disciples only needed to join the work God was doing.
q: Do you still think “the time has not come”?
Will you ask God to open your eyes so that you see the “harvest” that is already ripe, already prepared, already before you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, open our eyes so that we no longer measure Your work by our own timetable. Let us see the harvest You have already prepared, and join Your work with obedient hearts. May we not rely on ourselves but work with You under Your guidance, reaping the fruit You have prepared. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything that I did.”
So when the Samaritans came to him, they begged him to stay with them. He stayed there two days.
Many more believed because of his word.
They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.”
b: This passage is the outburst point of the Samaritan revival: a woman who had been ashamed and avoided people became the one who led a whole city to Christ. This is no coincidence; it is the power of God's salvation.

The text first says, “From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified.” She was a woman with a failed marriage, foolish choices, an unbearable past, and rejection. In human eyes she was unworthy, unqualified, and unsuitable to bear witness. But in God's eyes her brokenness was exactly the vessel for testimony.
She had no Bible degree, no preaching skills, no religious credentials; she had only one thing: “Jesus saw me and did not reject me.”
And with this declaration she made a whole city begin to long for Jesus.
True testimony is not “how strong I am” but “how He became my salvation in my weakness.”

So the people came to Jesus and “asked him to stay with them.” This was a deep longing: they did not just want to know about Him; they wanted to know Him personally. They did not just hear the woman's story; they longed to meet the Savior in person.
Jesus agreed: “He stayed there two days.” He does not refuse to be longed for; He gladly stays in hearts that seek Him.

Then the text says, “Many more believed because of his word.” The woman's testimony brought people to Jesus, but what truly made them believe was Jesus' word. Testimony gets attention, but Jesus' word changes lives.
The woman was like a “bridge,” and Jesus is the “road of life.”

Finally, the people said a beautiful thing to the woman: “It is no longer because of your speaking that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves.” This does not deny her but marks the next step of spiritual growth: from hearing others' testimony to meeting the Lord for oneself.

They went on: “We know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.” This is the core of the whole story. The woman thought He was a prophet, the people began to listen to Him, and finally the whole city proclaimed Him the redeeming Lord.
Prejudice collapsed, religious barriers vanished, shame was driven away by the light, and now a whole city had met Christ.
A broken woman brought revival to a city; a shameful story became a vessel of salvation; a seemingly powerless life became the key to the harvest of God's kingdom.
This is how wonderfully God works.
q: Are you willing to open up your story and become a bridge for others to meet Jesus?
When was the last time you “heard the Lord for yourself”? What did He say to you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for using our weakness as an outlet for Your power. Let us, like this woman, boldly share how You saw us, touched us, and renewed us. And help us not only to hear the testimony of others but to meet You ourselves and recognize You as the Savior of our lives. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: After the two days he went out from there and went into Galilee.
For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.
So when he came into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all the things that he did in Jerusalem at the feast, for they also went to the feast.
b: Jesus stayed two days in Samaria, sowing seeds of the gospel, and many believed because of His word. After two days He left there and went on to Galilee. By ordinary reasoning, one's own country should be the easiest place to be received, yet Jesus said something surprising:
“A prophet has no honor in his own country.”
These words point to a deep truth about human nature: the more familiar something is, the easier it is to take lightly; the more we see it every day, the more we take it for granted.

The people of Galilee had watched Jesus grow up. They saw Him as a carpenter, living an ordinary life like anyone else. When He began to do miracles and speak the truth, it was hard for them to see Him as the Savior sent from God.
They thought they knew Him, but they had never truly known Him.
Familiarity brings a kind of covering that keeps people from seeing the truth. This is why Jesus emphasized that true knowing does not come from distance, but from an open heart.

Yet Scripture goes on to say that when He came to Galilee, “the Galileans received him, having seen all the things that he did in Jerusalem.” In other words, they received Him because they had “seen miracles.” But this is not the deepest faith, because it is built on “outward sight” rather than on “knowing who He really is within.”
The Samaritans' faith came because of His word; the Galileans' welcome came because of His works.
The Samaritans saw His heart; the Galileans saw His power.
The Samaritans said, “He told me everything that I did”; the Galileans said, “We saw the miracles He did.”
The difference is great.
This reminds us that true faith is not because of miracles, but because He is Lord. True worship is not because of what He can do, but because of who He is.
If people only chase miracles, they easily lose their focus; if they truly see Jesus, they will receive Him in spirit and in truth.
When Jesus left Samaria, He was held back by hearts that were hungry for Him; when Jesus returned to Galilee, He was welcomed with curiosity and excitement.
The difference is the difference between life and form, between hunger and habit, between a door thrown open and a door left half open.
q: Is your faith built on “seeing miracles,” or on “knowing Jesus”?
Are you willing to ask God for a heart that is not numbed by familiarity, but hungers for Him every day?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, keep our hearts, so that we do not lose our reverence and hunger for You just because we are “familiar with You.” May we receive You not only because of what You have done, but because we know You as the Lord of life. Build our faith on truth, knowledge, and obedience, rather than on miracles and outward feelings. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus came therefore again to Cana of Galilee, where he made the water into wine. There was a certain nobleman whose son was sick at Capernaum.
When he heard that Jesus had come out of Judea into Galilee, he went to him, and begged him that he would come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
Jesus therefore said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe.”
b: After returning to Galilee, Jesus came again to Cana, where He had performed His first miracle. His disciples knew this place well, but this time He faced a man from a completely different background: a “nobleman,” a member of the local political and powerful class.
This nobleman's son lay sick at Capernaum, “at the point of death.” No parent can calmly face a dying child, so he set aside his status, his dignity, and his position for one purpose: to seek Jesus.

He “heard” that Jesus had come into Galilee, and he set out at once. He did not weigh the distance, did not worry whether his position made it fitting, did not care what others would think, because when life comes to the edge, a person is left with one thing that matters most: finding the Lord who can save.
His faith had two levels:
First, he believed Jesus could heal. This is why he was willing to travel so far to Cana.
Second, he thought Jesus had to “come down” to Capernaum in order to heal. His faith was sincere, but not complete; he believed God could act, yet still limited how God should act by his own way.
So he begged Jesus to “come down,” as if Jesus must be at the child's side in order to heal.
After hearing his urgent plea, Jesus answered with a surprising word:
“Unless you see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe.”
This was not a refusal, but a pointing out of a problem common to many at that time: their faith needed to “see,” rather than to “believe.”

Jesus was not rebuking the nobleman's anxiety, but lifting his knowledge of God. He wanted this father to know that God is not limited by form, circumstance, distance, or method. True faith is not only believing that God can act, but believing that however God acts, it is good and powerful.
Here Jesus was preparing to lead the nobleman into a deeper faith: not relying on miracles seen with the eyes, but relying on the word of God.
True faith is not believing after seeing, but believing because of His word.
True faith is not demanding that God work our way, but being willing to yield to God's way.
True faith is not holding on to our own methods, but holding on to the word of Jesus.
This passage is the beginning of a journey of faith, and in the next passage Jesus will lead this father deeper still, into a wonderful journey of “walking by faith, not by sight.”
q: Do you also often expect to “see” before you feel secure?
Are you willing to ask God to help you believe His word beyond what you can see?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, lead us into real faith, believing not only after we see Your works, but because of Your word. Help us lay down the ways we think things should go, and believe that Your ways are higher than our ways. May we, like this father, still come close to You in the midst of difficulty. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: The nobleman said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”
Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way.
b: This passage takes us into a father's deepest heartache, and shows us how Jesus, with a single word, brought him from despair into hope.
The nobleman begged Jesus again: “Sir, come down before my child dies.” His words carried three strong emotions:
1. Urgent love: “Sir, come down”
Whatever his position, a father's heart breaks the same way. When his own child is about to die, status no longer matters, face no longer matters; only the child's life matters.
2. Deep fear: “before my child dies”
He was racing against time. His anguish was so great it almost shattered him, afraid that Jesus would not arrive in time, would not be able to save.
3. Limited faith: “come down”
He believed Jesus could heal, yet still thought Jesus had to be there in person. His faith was sincere, but still carried human limits.
But Jesus wanted to bring him into a deeper faith: not believing in “how” God acts, but believing that what God says is done.

So Jesus said, “Go your way. Your son lives.” This sentence is the most pivotal moment in the whole story. Jesus did not follow the nobleman's method, nor go down with him; what He gave was not an action but a word, a word enough to heal a life, change reality, turn circumstances around, and bring hope.
For the nobleman, this was a crossroads of faith: would he believe the crisis his eyes could see, or the promise spoken from Jesus' mouth?
If he had stayed in Cana and not gone, he would not have received the fruit of faith; if he had doubted because he could not see a miracle, he would have stayed where he was.
But Scripture says: “The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way.”
This is the miracle of faith: he did not see his son healed, did not receive any news, did not see any evidence, but he “believed the word that Jesus spoke.”
Believed what? Not feelings, not signs, not circumstances, but the word of Jesus.
He went home carrying the word of Jesus, not the action of Jesus.
This is mature faith: not believing only after seeing, but believing because of His word.
The lesson Jesus wanted the nobleman to learn is also the one He wants us to learn:
• Not relying on what can be seen
• Not being frightened by circumstances
• Not limiting God by our own way
• Not demanding that God work by our methods
• Simply believing that what He says is true and reliable
In the moment that man turned and walked back, he was walking on a true “road of faith.” Although he had not yet seen the result, the word of Jesus was already accomplished.
q: What is the thing you are facing now that “seems too late”?
Are you willing to believe the word of Jesus over your fears and limits, and walk back into your daily life carrying His word?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, let us be like this father: not overwhelmed by the crisis before us, but choosing to believe Your word. Lead us to build our faith on Your word rather than on circumstances. If You speak a word, we are willing to go back in faith and walk on the road of Your promise. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: As he was now going down, his servants met him and reported, saying “Your child lives!”
So he inquired of them the hour when he began to get better. They said therefore to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him.”
So the father knew that it was at that hour in which Jesus said to him, “Your son lives.” He believed, as did his whole house.
This is again the second sign that Jesus did, having come out of Judea into Galilee.
b: This passage leads us to see the journey of faith from “hearing” to “believing,” then to “confirmation” and “passing on.” Through a miracle of healing at a distance, Jesus brought salvation to an entire family.
After believing the word of Jesus, the nobleman “went down”: he no longer insisted that Jesus go with him, and no longer insisted on his own way. All he carried was one sentence: “Your son lives.”

On his way back, “his servants met him.” He had not yet reached home, and the miracle had already traveled faster than he! God's work is never limited by distance, nor delayed by time. Because of one word from Him, life, change, healing, and transformation come.

The servants said, “Your son lives.” This meant not only that the child was healed, but that God had answered his faith. The father immediately asked, “At what hour did he begin to get better?” Not out of doubt, but because he longed for confirmation: was that moment exactly when Jesus spoke?

The servants answered, “Yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” The “seventh hour” was about one o'clock in the afternoon, and that was exactly when Jesus told the nobleman, “Your son lives.”
When he compared the times, he knew that his son's healing was not coincidence, but the fulfillment of the Lord's word.
It was not good timing, not natural recovery of the body, but the word of Jesus bringing a change of life.
So the father was deeply convinced: “This was the Lord's doing.”
Scripture says: “He believed, as did his whole house.” This faith was not because of the healing itself, but because he saw God's faithfulness, truth, power, and the authority of His word.
This is a beautiful spiritual order: the father first believed the word of Jesus, the word of Jesus was fulfilled, the father was assured of God's work, and his whole household was saved as a result.
A father's faith brought faith to the home. The change of a family begins with one heart willing to believe.

Finally, Scripture says, “This is again the second sign that Jesus did, having come out of Judea into Galilee.” The first sign was at Cana in Galilee, turning water into wine and filling the feast with joy; the second was at Cana in Galilee, healing with a word and bringing life.
One sign brought joy, the other brought faith; at the core of both signs is this: the word of Jesus is true, His word has power, and His word can change lives.
q: Are you willing, like this father, to hold on to one word of Jesus and let His word overcome your fear?
Do you long for your family to know the Lord together? Are you willing to be the one who leads “the whole household” to believe?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your word carries power, and with one word You can change our lives. Teach us to be like this father, believing not by sight but because of Your word. Let our faith also bring blessing to our families, so that our homes may come to know You and experience You together. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: After these things, there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches.
In these lay a great multitude of those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed, waiting for the moving of the water;
b: The scene shifts from Galilee back to Jerusalem. Jesus came not for religious ceremony, but for human need: He went to a place full of brokenness and pain, the pool beside Bethesda.

The name “Bethesda” means “house of grace” or “place of mercy.” In reality, it had become a gathering place for countless broken lives. Under its five porches lay a multitude of sick people: the blind, the lame, and the withered.
They represent different struggles of life:
The blind: unable to see direction, unable to see hope, unable to see the works of God. This is the loss of the soul's way.
The lame: wanting to walk but unable, wanting to change but without strength, wanting to stand but unsteady. This is the powerlessness of life.
The withered: inwardly drained of vitality, life used up, the inner person worn away. This is the dryness of the soul.
This was a place that looked forgotten by God, yet Jesus chose to walk into it.
He did not stand in the temple to preach, nor perform miracles amid a lively crowd, but went to the most overlooked, darkest, most painful corner.
Because He did not come for the righteous; He came for the broken, the helpless, and the disappointed.
No pain is too deep for Jesus to draw near; no life is too messy for Jesus to renew; no person is too weak for Him to stretch out His hand.
He walked into Bethesda to show us that God's mercy is not far away; His love comes toward us.
This passage also reminds us that everyone's life has “Bethesda porch” seasons: unable to see hope, unable to walk, dry within.
But Jesus will walk into your porch, into your difficulty, into your darkness, into the place that hurts you most.
He does not ask you to put yourself in order before coming; He comes to the place of your failure to touch you.
His mercy is that deep.
q: Which places in your life are like the Bethesda porches: unable to see, unable to walk, dry and weary?
Do you believe that Jesus is walking toward that place, looking for you, seeing you, and wanting to touch you personally?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for walking into the weakest, most weary, and most broken places of our lives. Let us see You in our own Bethesda porches and be strengthened again by You. May Your mercy come and restore our eyes, our steps, and our inner life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: In these lay a great multitude of those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed, waiting for the moving of the water;
b: The sick beside the pool of Bethesda were “waiting for the moving of the water.” They believed that when the water was stirred, the first one to step in would be healed. So the whole pool became a “place of waiting”: waiting for something good to happen, waiting for a chance, waiting for luck, waiting for the right time, yet often meeting endless disappointment.

This is a picture of human nature. When life gets stuck, we too often stay in “waiting”: waiting for circumstances to improve, for problems to disappear on their own, for someone to help, for a better opportunity, forgetting that our real hope is not “the moving of the water,” but Jesus, who comes to us on His own initiative.
Here was a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years. “Thirty-eight years” is not a day, not a month, not even a year… but the pain of a whole generation.

For Israel this number is deeply symbolic: Israel wandered thirty-eight years in the wilderness, trapped in a cycle of unbelief, powerlessness, repetition, and stagnation. Now a man had been trapped in his own “wilderness” for thirty-eight years.

He had not just happened to be sick for a few days; he had been stuck in hopelessness for most of his life. He lay in the same place, looked at the same crowd, held the same expectation, and went through the same disappointment.
We can imagine his heart:
• He had hoped
• He had been disappointed
• Then he went numb
• Finally he stopped in a powerlessness he had “gotten used to”
Thirty-eight years of pain was not only a sickness of the body, but a paralysis of the soul: a weariness of no longer having hope for the future, no strength for change, no expectation for life.
Yet Jesus came to him. Not because of his faith, nor because he still had strength to seek, but because Jesus looks for the most helpless with His eyes.
In a crowd of sick people, He saw the one who had been sick longest, deepest, and with the least hope. He went especially to him.
Because Jesus does not choose the people with the most faith to heal; He chooses the people with the least strength to show grace.
His grace does not respond to human ability, but comes to human weakness. His healing is not for those who “can walk,” but for those who “cannot walk.”
Jesus saw not only thirty-eight years of illness, but the disappointment, helplessness, and loneliness piled up in those years. He did not despise him; He chose to draw near.

This verse reminds us that life can sometimes get stuck in a “thirty-eight years” pattern: repeating, powerless, trapped, unchanging, waiting for a chance. But the mercy of Jesus is always greater than our powerlessness. He will walk into our Bethesda porch, to the longest, deepest, most painful place in us, and stretch out His hand to us.
q: Is there also some “thirty-eight years” in your life, a place long trapped, repeatedly powerless, no longer expecting change?
Do you believe that Jesus is coming toward that place, to see you personally, touch you, and make you stand again?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for not forgetting the thirty-eight years in our lives. Come to us Yourself, see us, and touch our weakness. May Your grace come and awaken us anew from powerlessness, hopelessness, and helplessness. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, “Do you want to be made well?”
The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, but while I’m coming, another steps down before me.”
b: In this passage Jesus did something profound and deeply moving: He went to this man who had been sick for thirty-eight years and spoke to him Himself.
Jesus was not simply passing by; He “saw” him. It was not a light glance, but He “knew that he had been sick for a long time.” He did not pity from afar, but drew near and spoke to him.
Among the crowded five porches Jesus saw him; among a crowd of broken people Jesus picked him out; in the most unnoticed corner, Jesus came to him.
This is the heart of the Lord: He looks for people's helplessness, not their performance; He responds to people's brokenness, not their ability.

Jesus asked him, “Do you want to be made well?” This is not a strange question, but one that reaches deep into the soul. Because true healing is not only the body standing up, but the heart being willing to stand.
After thirty-eight years of being stuck, this man had grown used to illness, used to weakness, used to powerlessness, used to depending on others, even used to disappointment.

Jesus' question is really asking: Are you willing to leave your old pattern? Are you willing to let go of the powerlessness you know so well? Are you willing to come out of the pain you have grown used to? Are you willing to pay a price for healing? Are you willing to begin a new life?
Healing is not cheap; healing means responsibility, freedom, growth, change. Not everyone wants to be healed. But Jesus wanted him to face his own heart.
Yet the sick man's answer exposed his true condition: not a lack of faith, but a heart trapped too long.

He said, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up.” His attention was still on “the water,” on “people,” on “opportunity.” Thirty-eight years of pain had made him believe:
• I need other people
• I have no one
• I will always be too late
• Others are always faster than I
• My fate depends on others' faces
• All I can do is wait
• I am powerless
What he answered was not “whether I want to be healed,” but “why I cannot be healed.”
He gave reasons; Jesus asked about desire. He spoke of difficulties; Jesus asked about longing. He described limits; Jesus looked for faith.

This answer shows us the deepest condition of a long-suffering soul: trapped long enough, one no longer has strength even to want healing; disappointed long enough, one no longer has courage to long for change; lonely long enough, even faith to move forward is stolen away.
But Jesus did not rebuke him. He did not come to demand that he have faith, but to bring the source of faith to him.
Jesus did not ask him to get to the pool by himself; Jesus wanted to bring life to him.

People think healing depends on the water, on opportunity, on others, on one's own effort; but Jesus says, “Not the water, but Me; not luck, but grace; not you crawling there, but Me coming to save you.”
This is the heart of grace: it is not man seeking God, but God coming to man.
q: Are there places in your life where you have “gotten used to powerlessness”?
Today, if Jesus asked you, “Do you want to be made well?”
How would you answer Him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for seeing our long-standing weakness and being willing to come to our deepest pain. Make us willing to answer Your question, to long for healing, to long to stand up, to long to walk into the new life You have prepared for us. May Your grace overcome our limits, and may Your power come upon our powerlessness. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.”
Immediately, the man was made well, and took up his mat and walked. Now it was the Sabbath on that day.
b: These two verses seem short, yet they hold profound spiritual truth: a paralytic of thirty-eight years had his whole life turned around by one word from Jesus.
Jesus did not discuss his reasons, analyze his difficulties, rebuke his powerlessness, tell him to try harder, or suggest how to get into the water faster.
Jesus went straight to the heart: “Arise.”
This was not a command but power; not a demand but grace; not pressure but release.
When Jesus said “Arise,” His word itself carried the power to arise. He was not telling a man who could not walk to walk, but using His word to enable a man who could not walk to walk.
Then He said, “Take up your mat, and walk.” These words carry even deeper meaning.
First, taking up the mat means leaving the past.
The mat was the symbol of his thirty-eight years: his failure, his habits, his limits, his weakness, his passivity, his past.

Jesus wanted him to pick up the past, gather it, and leave it, no longer lying back down in the old life. The easiest temptation for a healed person is to return to the old life, old attitudes, old habits. By telling him to take up his mat, Jesus was reminding him: “Do not go back. You are no longer who you were.”
Second, taking up the mat means testimony.
The picture of him carrying his mat was the most concrete evidence of his healing. Others did not need him to say much; the mat in his hands was his testimony.
Third, “walk” means beginning a new journey.
Healing is not the goal; healing is the beginning. This was a road he had never walked, because for thirty-eight years he had not walked at all.
Jesus did not just tell him to get up; He told him to begin the first real walk of his life, not by his own strength, but by the word of Jesus, the grace of Jesus, the power of Jesus.
Then Scripture says: “Immediately, the man was made well.” Not in a day, not in a week, not after a year of rehabilitation, but “immediately.”
Human limits cannot limit the word of God; the length of time cannot limit the depth of grace. Thirty-eight years of pain was turned around by one word from Jesus.

“He took up his mat and walked.” This is the most beautiful picture of grace: the one who lay down stood up; the one who could not walk walked; the one trapped in the past left it; the one without hope began a new journey.
This is also what Jesus does in each of our lives. He does not merely help us solve problems; He makes us stand up, leave the old life, and walk toward the road He has prepared.

He does not tell us to “try to be better,” but by His word moves us “from cannot to can.” He does not tell us to “hang on,” but to “arise.” He does not tell us to “forget the past,” but to “pick up the past” so that it becomes a testimony rather than a chain.
q: Are you willing to let Jesus say “Arise” to some area of your life that has been “paralyzed” for a long time?
Are you willing to take up your mat, the past that once bound you, and begin to walk a new journey?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that with one word You can change our lives. Let us hear Your “Arise” spoken to us, and awaken us from powerlessness. Help us pick up the past and not lie back down in the old life, but walk the new road You have prepared for us. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: So the Jews said to him who was cured, “It is the Sabbath. It is not lawful for you to carry the mat.”
He answered them, “He who made me well said to me, ‘Take up your mat and walk.’”
Then they asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ‘Take up your mat and walk’?”
But he who was healed didn’t know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, a crowd being in the place.
b: This passage shows us a deep spiritual conflict: Jesus gives life, but religion only watches the rules; Jesus renews life, but religion cannot see the healing; Jesus brings grace, but religion only says, “It is not lawful.”
1. The eyes of religion: unable to see life, seeing only rules

That day was the Sabbath. To the Jews this meant law, custom, tradition, regulation. They saw a man who had been sick thirty-eight years stand up and walk carrying his mat, yet did not ask him, “How were you healed?” They were not amazed: “You are actually well!” They did not rejoice: “A miracle has happened to you!”
They could only say, “It is not lawful.” What they cared about was not whether a person's life had been restored, but whether he had stepped on a rule.
Religion keeps people from seeing the work of God, because religion puts the focus on “methods,” not on “life.”
2. The healed man: simple obedience to the One who healed him
This newly healed man did not understand theology, nor the details of the Sabbath rules; he was sure of only one thing: the One who made me well is the One I am willing to obey.
He said, “He who made me well, the same said to me, ‘Take up your mat, and walk.’”
He meant: “All my life I lay down, and only He told me to arise; all my life I could not walk, and only He let me walk; whatever He tells me to do, I do.”
This is “obedience of life,” not “obedience to rules.” He obeyed because he had met Jesus, not because he feared breaking the law.
In contrast to the coldness of the religious, this healed man showed a simple, real, open heart.
3. The Pharisees' focus: not Jesus, but “who broke the rule”
The religious did not ask, “Who healed you?” They asked:
“Who is the man who said to you, ‘Take up your mat, and walk’?”
They were not looking for a Savior; they were looking for a criminal. Not for the source of life, but for a breach in the rules.
This is the nature of religion: unable to see the grace of God, yet always looking for a reason to accuse.
4. The healed man did not know where Jesus was
Scripture says, “He who was healed didn't know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn.”
Jesus did not stay on the stage, nor ask for the crowd's attention; He needed no applause, fame, or spotlight, but only wanted to take away that man's pain.
Jesus does not build a reputation for Himself; He builds new life for people.
He did not perform miracles to be seen; He performed miracles so that people would have life.

Although this paralytic did not know who Jesus was, his life had already been touched by Jesus. This is the starting point of grace: often we do not yet know Him, yet He has already loved us first, healed us first, sought us first.
q: Have you ever stopped obeying Jesus because “others said it was not allowed”?
Today, will you ask God to let you focus on the work of life He is doing, rather than on people's religious judgments?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, guard our hearts from falling into the eyes of religion, seeing only rules and not life. Let us, like this healed man, simply follow Your voice, because only You bring life. May we not be bound by people's comments, but be carried forward by Your grace. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Afterward Jesus found him in the temple, and said to him, “Behold, you are made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.”
The man went away, and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.
b: This passage unveils a deep spiritual truth: Jesus cares not only about our outward healing, but even more about our inner life; He does not only want us to walk, but to walk the right road.
1. Jesus came to find him again, on His own initiative
Scripture says, “Afterward Jesus found him in the temple.” This was not accidental, but deliberate. Though the healed man had received bodily freedom, he had not yet received guidance for his life.
The first time Jesus met him at Bethesda; the second time Jesus met him in the temple. This shows the Lord's heart toward us:
He finds us not only in our place of pain, but also guides us after we are restored.
Jesus does not only heal a person's past; He also cares for a person's future.
2. Jesus told him an important truth
Jesus said, “Behold, you are made well. Sin no more.” This was not because his earlier illness had necessarily been caused by sin, but to remind him:
After the body is healed, life must move toward renewal. Grace does not let people continue the old life; grace lets people begin a new life.
“Sin no more” is not moral preaching; Jesus was saying to him, “Do not return to the old ways that dried up your life, made you weak, and kept you far from God.”
Jesus knows that some pain is caused not only by outward circumstances, but by a wrong direction within the heart.
So after healing him He gave a word of life as a reminder:
Do not walk again toward the road that makes you suffer. I want to heal not only your legs, but your heart.
Jesus also said, “so that nothing worse happens to you.” This was not a threat or a curse, but a gentle warning:
If life does not turn toward God, even when the body is well, the soul can fall into deeper bondage.
True freedom is not being able to walk, but truly walking in the way of God.
3. After knowing it was Jesus, the man did what he could

Scripture says, “The man went away, and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.” Some criticize this man as having “betrayed” Jesus, but from the context he was simply stating the fact.
He had been asked, “Who is the man who said to you, ‘Take up your bed and walk’?” He did not know. When Jesus met him again, he knew. So he told them.
This was not informing on Jesus, but testifying. For one just healed, it is not easy to discern the conflict between religion and Jesus, but he did at least one right thing:
He acknowledged that it was Jesus who made him well.
This is the simplest and truest beginning of faith.
4. What this passage reminds us
1. Jesus cares not only about our suffering, but also about the road we walk in the future.
2. Healing is a beginning, not an end.
3. True grace leads people toward a better life, not back to their old ways.
4. “Sin no more” is a reminder of love, not a burden of law.
5. For one touched by Jesus, the greatest testimony is to acknowledge: He changed me.
q: In what matter is Jesus saying to you, “Sin no more”?
Are you willing to hand that area over to Him again, and let Him lead you into a renewed life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for not only healing us but also guiding our lives. After we receive grace, let us not walk back on the old road, but walk in the path of Your light. Help us hear Your reminder and respond to You with reverence and love, so that our lives are no longer bound by sin but live in Your true freedom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: For this cause the Jews persecuted Jesus, and sought to kill him, because he did these things on the Sabbath.
But Jesus answered them, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.”
For this cause therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
b: This passage reveals the true heart of the conflict between Jesus and the religious leaders: not the mat, not the Sabbath, not form, but who He is.
1. The reaction of the religious: unable to see grace, seeing only rules
Scripture says, “For this cause the Jews persecuted Jesus, because he did these things on the Sabbath.” What things? Healing a man who had been sick thirty-eight years so that he could walk.
But the religious did not rejoice at this. What they saw was not life restored, but a rule touched.
To them,
• the Sabbath mattered more than people's pain
• tradition mattered more than life
• the letter mattered more than grace
Religion makes people unable to see God, even when a miracle is right before their eyes.
When a heart is bound by “methods,” it loses the heart of God.
2. Jesus' answer: the Father is working, and I am working
Jesus did not explain, argue, or retreat; He directly declared the source of His action:
“My Father is working until now, and I am working.”
These words shook the whole religious world.
Jesus meant: the Father's love never rests, so I do not stop healing. The Father's mercy does not pause for the Sabbath, and I will not stop showing grace.

God does not “stop loving people” on the Sabbath; God “loves people especially” on the Sabbath. He is not idle; He is doing work that human eyes cannot see: upholding all things, showing mercy to the world, seeking the lost, healing the broken.
What Jesus did was not destroying the law, but revealing the heart behind the law: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).
Those who truly know God understand that God's work is never to stop people's lives, but to restore them.
3. The religious reaction grew fiercer
“The Jews sought all the more to kill him.” Why?
Because He did two things they could not accept:
1. He walked in grace, not bound by rules.
This threatened the religious, because grace tears down human control.
2. He called God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.
Jesus was not a prophet, a teacher, or a religious leader; He declared Himself the Son of God, of the same essence as the Father.
This was what the Jewish leaders could least accept, because if He were truly God, their entire religious structure would have to submit to Him.
Jesus' declaration challenged not only the understanding of the Sabbath, but the very core of the whole religious system.
He did not come to patch up religion; He came to reveal the Father.
He did not come to maintain tradition; He came to bring out truth.
He did not come to become part of religion; He came to be the Lord of life.
4. Reminders this passage gives us
1. The eyes of religion see faults but cannot see grace.
2. Jesus' actions followed entirely the Father's heart, not human rules.
3. Those who truly know Jesus focus on life, not form.
4. Jesus is not an ordinary teacher; He is the Son of God, sharing the Father's glory and honor.
5. If we are to follow Jesus, we must also overcome human opinion and focus on the Father's will.
q: Do you sometimes also treat religious form as more important than people's lives?
Will you ask God to help you know His heart more, so that you walk in grace rather than in human rules?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help us not to fall into the eyes of religion, seeing rules but not Your heart. Let us, like Jesus, take Your will as our road and Your love as our strength. Make us unafraid of people's comments and not bound by tradition, but living in the freedom of Your truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus therefore answered them, “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.
For the Father has affection for the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does. He will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel.
b: These two verses are central to understanding the relationship between Jesus and the Father, and are among the most important revelations in the whole Gospel of John. Here Jesus unveils the deepest reason behind all His actions, teaching, miracles, and mission: He lived completely within the Father's will.
1. Jesus' obedience was not reluctant, but a oneness of love
Jesus said, “The Son can do nothing of himself.” This is not a lack of ability but an expression of relationship.
He meant: “I do not do what I myself want, but only what the Father wants.”
This is complete oneness: not forced obedience, not submission under pressure, but alignment born out of love.
He did not do His own will, but let the Father's will rule fully within Him.
This lets us see that in Jesus' life there was no “I,” only “the Father.” It is not that He could not think, but that He did not want His own will to override the Father's.
He was completely self-denied, completely humble, completely yielded, and therefore He could fully reveal the Father.
Everything He did was like the Father; every word He spoke came from the Father; His attitude, His heart, His actions were all the Father's heart.
2. Jesus saw what the Father was doing, and followed
“But what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.”
Jesus' ministry did not depend on judgment, experience, or method, but on “seeing.”
He did not look at circumstances, needs, or opportunities; He looked at “what the Father is doing now.”
He did not rely on analysis but on receiving; not on Himself but on the Father.
This is the most important secret of spiritual life: ministry with true power follows what the Father is doing.
When the Father wanted to heal, Jesus healed; when the Father wanted to teach, Jesus taught; when the Father wanted to seek the one who was lost, Jesus went toward him.
He never ran ahead of the Father, and never lagged behind. This is perfect synchrony.
It is also the most important example for us in learning to follow Jesus: turning our focus from “what shall I do?” to “what is the Father doing now?”
3. The Father loves the Son and shows Him all that He does

Verse 20 says, “For the Father has affection for the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does.” Jesus could see the Father not by effort, but because the Father took the initiative to reveal Himself to Him.
This is not a secret of office; it is the result of intimacy.
The Father loves the Son, so He opens His heart to the Son. The Son loves the Father, so He completely follows His will.
This is the most perfect relationship in heaven: love brings revelation, revelation brings obedience, obedience brings power.
Today the Holy Spirit likewise reveals the Father's heart to us, guides us into the truth, and leads us to know the way we should walk.
The Father is not stingy; He is willing to show His heart to all who draw near to Him.
4. The Father will show Him greater works

Jesus said the Father would show Him “greater works,” greater than healing the paralytic, greater than the Sabbath conflict, pointing to redemption, forgiveness of sins, resurrection, judgment, and eternal life.
These things would make the world “marvel,” and would also unveil Jesus' true identity: He is not merely a worker of miracles; He is the Lord who holds life.
q: Which do you ask most often today: “What shall I do?” or “What is the Father doing now?”
Are you willing, like Jesus, to lay down your own thoughts and let the Father's will be the direction of your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, make our hearts like Jesus', not doing our own will but seeking only Yours. Let our eyes see what You are doing and our ears hear Your voice, so that our lives walk in step with You. May our hearts be simple, humble, and emptied of self, so that we can receive Your greater purposes. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he desires.
For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son,
that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father. He who doesn’t honor the Son doesn’t honor the Father who sent him.
b: These three verses show us the peak revelation of Jesus' identity: He is not only a healer, prophet, teacher, or mediator of creation; He is the Lord who holds life and judgment. Without this passage, our knowledge of Jesus would stop at His miracles; but through it we see His very nature: He is the source of life.
1. Jesus does not only heal people; He makes them live
“For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life.”
Here Jesus declares a truth beyond the universe: He does not merely heal the sick, He is the Lord who raises the dead.

In the Old Testament, only God can raise the dead (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6). Now Jesus says, “As the Father, so also I.” He is not imitating the Father; He shares the Father's power, nature, and action.
The healing of the paralytic was only the beginning; Jesus wanted humanity to know that He did not come to mend life, but to give life.
He did not come to make the old life a bit better, but to make dead lives alive.
Those who truly know Jesus do not merely ask Him for help, but submit to Him, because He is the Master of life.
2. The authority of judgment is entirely in Jesus' hands
Verse 22 speaks weightily: “For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son.”
Note the word: all. Not partial, not shared, not cooperative, but entrusted completely to the Son.
What is judgment? It is the highest authority in the universe. Only God can judge people; yet the Father gave this highest authority to Jesus.
This proves that Jesus is not a created being, not a created spirit, not an angel, not one of His creatures. He is God, equal with the Father; otherwise judgment could not be placed in His hands.
We often treat Jesus as friend, healer, provider, and helper, but here Jesus reminds us that He is also Judge. Every motive, action, direction, and focus in life will finally stand before Him.
This is not meant to frighten, but to remind us to align our lives with His heart.
3. Honoring and revering Jesus is honoring the Father
Verse 23 says, “that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father.”
This was a shocking declaration to the Jews, because in the Jewish faith, reverence for God is the most untouchable core.
But Jesus said, “As you revere the Father, so revere Me.” There is only one possibility: Jesus shares the same divine glory with the Father.
He is not merely honored; He is to be worshiped. He is not like God; He is God.
Then He said, “He who doesn't honor the Son doesn't honor the Father who sent him.” In other words:
To reject Jesus is to reject God. To belittle Jesus is to belittle God. To make light of Jesus' words is to make light of God's voice.

There is no middle ground. To choose Jesus, we must revere Him with all our hearts. He is Lord, not a helper; He is King, not a consultant; He is the source of life, not an option for times of weakness.
This passage brings us back to the most important focus: everything in life begins with Jesus and must be aligned to Him.
q: In your daily life, do you put Jesus in the “helper's place” or in “the place of Lord”?
Today, will you place Him back on the throne of glory?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for placing the authority of life and judgment in Jesus' hands, so that in Him we may know You. Give us the right reverence for Jesus in our hearts, not treating Him as optional, but truly letting Him be Lord. May our lives be renewed in His light and led in His truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: “Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.
b: This verse is one of the clearest, most precious, and most direct gospel declarations in the whole Gospel of John. Jesus opens with the solemn “Most certainly I tell you,” showing that what He is about to declare is the greatest truth in heaven, the very heart of the gospel of God's kingdom.
This is not a guess, not a hope, not a conditional possibility, but a certain, real, eternal promise.
1. Eternal life is not a future thing, but a present receiving
Jesus said, “He who hears my word, and believes him who sent me, has eternal life.”
Note that He does not say “will have in the future,” nor “may have,” but: has it now (have eternal life).

Eternal life is not a life that begins only after death; eternal life is a life received now. From the moment you believe in Jesus, eternal life enters you, your relationship with God is restored, you receive new life, and you are brought into the eternal kingdom.
Eternal life is not a length of time but a quality of life: being joined to God, being with God, living in God's life.
So eternal life is a “present tense” reality.
2. Not coming into judgment: salvation is not left hanging, but already settled
Jesus said, “doesn't come into judgment.”
What is condemnation? It is the final verdict on a sinner before God.
But Jesus said, “If you hear my word and believe the Father who sent me, you will not be condemned.”
Why? Because you now stand under another judgment: not the judgment of sin, but the judgment of grace.
Jesus did not make your sins a little less; He moved you out from the death sentence of sin. He did not make you barely meet the standard; He brought you into complete forgiveness.
Not coming into judgment is not because you are good enough, but because Jesus bore the judgment of sin in your place.
This is the heart of the cross.
3. Already passed out of death into life: salvation is an actual transfer
Jesus said, “has passed out of death into life.”
Note three key words:
Already: not waiting for the future, nor achieved step by step, but happening now.
Out of death: the original does not mean “leaving death,” but “being pulled out of the realm of death.”
Into life: not “living a little better,” but being brought into the kingdom of life.
This is not a metaphor but spiritual reality: those who believe in Jesus are transferred from the kingdom of death (darkness, sin, destruction) into the kingdom of life (light, grace, eternity).
This is a “change of position,” not an “effort of behavior.” A transfer of identity, not moral progress.
You do not slowly come alive; you are brought into life by God in one moment.
This is the greatest, most thorough, most profound change in the universe.
4. Three assurances this verse gives us
1. Assurance of eternal life: not waiting for death, but possessing it now.
2. Assurance of no condemnation: not depending on your performance, but on Jesus' redemption.
3. Assurance of transfer of life: not gradual, but already out of death and into life.
We no longer stand in the kingdom of death, nor before the judgment seat of sin; we already stand in life, light, and grace.
This is the heart of the gospel: believing in Jesus does not merely change a life, but changes life itself.
q: Do you truly believe that you have eternal life now, that you are no longer condemned, and that you have already passed out of death into life?
Are you willing to rest your whole life in this assurance?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your Son has brought us eternal life, so that we no longer wander between sin and condemnation. Thank You that in the moment we believed we had already passed out of death into life. Help us live every day in the assurance of this salvation, and fill our hearts with peace, gratitude, and reverence. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Most certainly I tell you, the hour comes, and now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live.
For as the Father has life in himself, even so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself.
He also gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is a son of man.
b: These three verses are among Jesus' deepest and most striking declarations of His identity. If John 5:24 showed us the assurance of salvation, then verses 25–27 show us the authority and power behind that salvation: Jesus not only gives eternal life, He is eternal life itself.
This passage tells us three key truths: the voice of Jesus raises the dead; the life of Jesus shares the same source as the Father's; and the authority of judgment is in Jesus' hands.
1. The dead will hear the voice of the Son of God (verse 25)
Jesus said, “An hour is coming, and now is.”
He was not speaking of the future resurrection (that is mentioned later); He was speaking of now: when He speaks, the dead can live.
The “dead” here means not only those whose bodies have died, but those who are already dead in spirit:
• those without hope
• those bound by sin
• those living in darkness
• those unresponsive to God
• those whose souls are numb
When Jesus' voice comes, dead souls awaken, cold hearts burn again, and broken people stand up anew.
His voice is not information; His voice is life.
Just as when He said “Arise” to the paralytic, that voice itself carried the power to arise, so today His voice still carries resurrection power.
He does not tell people to change; He makes them live.
Anyone who hears His voice, however dry their life, can come alive.
2. The life of Jesus shares the same source as the Father's (verse 26)
“For as the Father has life in himself, even so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself.”
Note the depth of this statement: Jesus was not given life; He has always had life.
His life is not created life, not dependent life, not life supplied from outside, but “self-existent, eternal” life.
This is an attribute unique to God (Exodus 3:14). Now Jesus says: as the Father has life in Himself, so the Son also.
This means that Jesus does not come near life; He is life itself (John 14:6). He does not share life; He is the source of life. He does not simply give life to people; He brings people into His life.
You live today not because of your effort, but because His life is already at work within you.
3. The authority of judgment is in Jesus' hands (verse 27)
“and he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is a son of man.”
Here Jesus reveals His dual identity: He is both the Son of God and “the Son of Man.”
Because He is the Son of Man, He can judge people, since He fully experienced all that people experience. Because He is the Son of God, He can judge, since He holds God's authority.
This authority was not seized by Him; it was given by the Father.
He is qualified to judge because He fully understands people; He is able to judge because He is by nature the Lord of life.
The authority of judgment is not to condemn those who believe in Him, but to show that the Master of life is He, and the authority of the universe is He.
This verse is not meant to make us afraid, but to make us revere, feel secure, and trust:
The Jesus you believe in is the Lord who holds life and judgment. His voice can raise the dead; His life can give you strength; His authority can protect you to the end.
q: Which word from Jesus do you most need to hear today, to make your heart “live” again?
Will you say in your struggle, “Lord, I want to hear Your voice and come alive again”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving the authority of life and judgment to Your Son, so that we know Jesus is not only our Savior but also the Lord of life. Let us hear His voice every day, so that our withered hearts may live. May we always live in the light and truth of His life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Don’t marvel at this, for the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice,
and will come out; those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.
b: These two verses bring us face to face with eternal reality: Jesus not only raises people in spirit from death, but will also, at the last day, raise all who have died in the body. The whole of John chapter 5 is a revelation of life, but at verses 28–29 Jesus directly declares the final judgment and the ultimate resurrection.
This is not a figure of speech or a symbol, but an unveiling of what will surely happen at the end.
1. The voice of Jesus has power to raise the dead from their graves (verse 28)
“The hour comes, in which all that are in the tombs will hear his voice.”
Verse 25 spoke of the “spiritually dead” who can hear the Lord's voice and live now, but here Jesus refers to the “bodily resurrection” at the last day.
In very clear words He declared that those who have died in the body will hear His voice again.
This is not fantasy, but an end that God has already decided.
No matter where the grave is, how long ago death came, whether the body has turned to dust, however many bodies the seas, the earth, and the depths have taken in,
when Jesus' voice sounds, people will rise.
This is the final proof that He is the Lord of life. He does not hold only the present; He holds eternity.
For those who believe in Him, this is hope; for those who reject Him, this is a shock.
But He said, “Don't marvel at this.” Because the gospel is life overcoming death; from the beginning God determined that people should live and not perish.
2. All will rise, but in different directions (verse 29)
“Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.”
This verse reveals a profound truth: resurrection is not a privilege of believers, but the destiny of all humanity.
But the outcome after resurrection differs:
• some “rise to life”
• some “rise to judgment”
What decides the direction? Not outward conduct, but the source of life: whether it is “from God” or “rejecting God.”
“Those who have done good rise to life”
“Doing good” does not mean being saved by our own good works, but living out goodness in the life of God, the natural fruit of the new life that comes from believing in Jesus.
When these stand before Jesus, the Lord of life, they enter eternal joy, light, rest, and glory.
“Those who have done evil rise to judgment”
“Doing evil” in the original does not mean occasional sin, but rejecting God's light, resisting God's life, and choosing to live in darkness.
These are not condemned for failing to do good, but for rejecting Jesus, rejecting the source of life, rejecting the Father's redemption.
Resurrection is not a choice; the direction after resurrection is the choice.
3. The judgment of resurrection reminds us: life is not only this life
Here Jesus draws our eyes from “the present” toward “eternity.”
If life were only a few decades, many things would not matter; but if life leads to eternity, every choice matters greatly.
He tells us:
• death is not the end
• the grave is not the finish
• resurrection is real
• eternity is certain
• everyone must finally face Jesus
• the direction of a whole life will be examined
This teaches us to live in reverence, because eternity is more real than the present; and to live in hope, because death cannot hold those who believe in Him.
Believers do not fear death, because resurrection belongs to us.
q: When you think of the day you will stand before Jesus, what do you most want to be commended for by Him?
Is there something you are willing to readjust today, so that you walk the road of “the resurrection of life”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us know the truth of resurrection and eternity. Help us live in reverence and in hope, not trapped by the brevity of this life, but seeing each day with eternal eyes. May our lives be fully aligned with Jesus, so that on the day of resurrection we may stand among the living. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.
b: This verse continues Jesus' deep revelation of His relationship with the Father, especially how He acts, how He judges, and how He decides everything. He emphasizes again that His ministry is not independent, self-directed, or self-reliant, but completely aligned with the Father's heart.
If the earlier verses (19–29) unveiled Jesus' identity and authority, this verse unveils the inner principle of Jesus' life: He has no will of His own.
This is the source of all His power and the foundation of all His authority.
1. Jesus declares again: I can do nothing of myself
He is not saying He lacks power, but that He refuses to act “independently of the Father.”
True power is not “I can,” but “I cannot of myself.”
Jesus' power flows from self-denial: He does not do what He Himself wants, only what the Father is doing.
This tells us: the more we are emptied of self, the more power we have; the less we rely on ourselves, the more God's work can be shown.
Jesus was not performing for us; He truly lived this way. In public and in private, in prayer and in action, every moment He depended on the Father.
He never departed from the Father's every thought and movement. His heart was completely aligned, completely humble, completely yielded.
This is His glory, and also His example.
2. Why is Jesus' judgment just?
He said, “As I hear, I judge.” He meant, “I do not judge by my own eyes; I judge according to what the Father says.”
Human judgment is often tinted with bias, limited by emotion, limited by vision, but Jesus' judgment comes entirely from the Father, so it is absolutely righteous.
He does not look at the outward appearance as people do; He looks at the heart through the Father's eyes.
He does not look at how people perform; He looks at whether their hearts are turned toward God.
His judgment is just because it is not affected by selfish interest, not swayed by human favor, not controlled by circumstances.
He stands completely on the Father's side.
3. He seeks not His own will, but the will of the Father
This sentence is the highest principle of Jesus' life and the true spiritual core:
“I seek not my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”
He is not saying He has no opinions, but that He lays down His own will completely so that the Father's will rules within Him.
This is not suppression, not loss of self, not passive compliance, but an active, joyful surrender full of love.
Jesus did not “have to obey”; He “gladly and willingly obeyed.”
Every day He walked on earth, He lived by this principle. His decisions, His steps, His ministry, His words, His attitude all came from one core:
“Father, whatever You want, I want.”
This is also why every judgment He made in this world was just, every healing was in line with God's heart, every word was like living water, and every step carried God's power.
Because He was not living out Himself, but living out the Father.
4. The deepest discipline this verse gives us
Jesus does not call us to become strong people; He calls us to become people “willing to lay down self.”
Spiritual power does not come from effort, but from surrender.
True freedom is not doing what we want, but truly living in the Father's will.
When we learn to be like Jesus:
• not relying on our own wisdom
• not relying on our own judgment
• not relying on our own methods
• not following our own will
but seeking the Father's heart and the Holy Spirit's leading,
we will see God's works, experience God's power, and live out God's glory.
q: Which area are you most prone to “rely on yourself” in today?
Are you willing to say to God in that matter, “Father, not my will, but Yours”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give us a heart like Jesus', seeking not our own will but Yours. Turn our eyes from ourselves toward You; let our ears hear Your voice; let our steps keep pace with You. May Your will be fully accomplished in our lives, and may our hearts be wholly yielded to You. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: “If I testify about myself, my witness is not valid.
It is another who testifies about me. I know that the testimony which he testifies about me is true.
b: In this passage Jesus begins to speak of the “source of His witness”: He is not making an empty claim to be the Son of God, nor testifying for Himself, saying, “This is who I am.” He unveils an extremely important spiritual principle: His identity is not self-promotion, but is testified to by the Father.
These words show us Jesus' humility, truthfulness, and reliability, and also how the Father bears witness through Jesus, so that the world may know His identity with certainty.
1. Jesus says He does not testify about Himself (verse 31)
He said, “If I testify about myself, my witness is not valid.”
Note that He is not saying His testimony is flawed, but that He chooses not to rely on His own testimony.
Why?
Because the principle of Jesus' life is: not speaking for Himself, not proving Himself, not seeking glory for Himself.
He is not trying to prove He is great; He is revealing the Father's heart.
He does not want people to believe His words; He wants people to see the Father's mark on Him.
Jesus does not market Himself, exalt Himself, beautify Himself, or advertise Himself.
All His glory points to the Father.
This is the exact opposite of the world's pattern. The world says, “Look at me, look at me, look at me.” But Jesus says, “Look at the Father, look at the Father, look at the Father.”
This is His self-denial: He does not live for Himself; He lives for the Father.
2. The Father is the One who gives the truest witness to Jesus (verse 32)
Jesus said, “It is another who testifies about me, and I know that the testimony which he testifies about me is true.”
He meant the Father. The Father Himself testified for Jesus, from beginning to end without gaps:
1. At Jesus' baptism, the Father's voice testified publicly
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). The people heard it with their own ears; heaven opened, the Spirit descended, and the Father Himself testified to His Son.
2. The miracles Jesus did are the Father's testimony

He would say later, “The works which I do, they testify about me” (John 5:36). The healing of the paralytic, sight for the blind, the calming of the storm, the raising of the dead: all are marks of the Father's authorization.
3. Jesus' teaching is also the Father's testimony to Him
What He said and taught were not His own words, but the Father's voice speaking through Him.
4. The cross and resurrection are the Father's final testimony
God declared through the resurrection that Jesus is truth, life, the Son of God, the King of kings.
The Father declared Jesus' identity by His own actions; Jesus did not need to prove Himself, because the Father proved Him personally.
3. Jesus' complete humility gives His witness absolute truthfulness
Jesus said His testimony is true not because He worked hard to persuade, but because the Father speaks for Him.
When a person does not speak for himself, the Father will speak for him.
When a person does not pursue his own glory, the Father will give him glory.
Jesus shows us the most beautiful spiritual pattern: true authority needs no self-exaltation, true identity needs no self-emphasis, and those who truly belong to God quietly leave the proving to God.
Jesus lived this life fully, and calls us to learn His pattern: not standing on our own, but standing on the Father's testimony.
q: In your life, are there areas where you badly want to “prove yourself”?
Today, are you willing to learn from Jesus, hand the “proving” over to the Father, and seek only His heart?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for personally testifying for Your Son, so that we can be sure Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life. Put Jesus' humility into our hearts, so that we do not prove ourselves by ourselves but rest in Your testimony. Let us learn from Him not to seek glory for ourselves, but to seek only Your will. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth.
But the testimony which I receive is not from man. However, I say these things that you may be saved.
He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.
b: In this passage Jesus mentions John the Baptist, pointing out the role John played and the value of his witness. But Jesus also unveils a deeper, more serious reality: the heart can love the light yet be unwilling to walk toward it; it can admire the voice of truth yet be unwilling to submit to Truth itself.
This passage is Jesus' gentle reminder and warning to the religious leaders of that day, and to each of us.
1. John bore witness to the truth (verse 33)
John the Baptist was a witness raised up by God; his purpose was not to exalt himself but to point to Jesus.
He proclaimed loudly, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).
The religious leaders had sent people to ask John, “Who are you?” (John 1:19).
